messages.content: Our public library is changing its Saturday hours and I have to post the notice. The facts: starting March 7, the library will close at 4 p.m. on Saturdays instead of 6 p.m., because of a staffing shortage. Book returns stay open 24 hours. Can you show me the same announcement in a few different registers so I can pick?

Same facts, four voices. Watch what changes: contractions, sentence length, and who the sentence is about.

**Formal** (for the printed bulletin and the board report):
"Effective Saturday, March 7, the library will conclude Saturday operations at 4:00 p.m., rather than 6:00 p.m., owing to a staffing shortage. The exterior book return will remain available at all hours."

**Neutral** (the website default):
"Starting Saturday, March 7, the library will close at 4 p.m. on Saturdays instead of 6 p.m. This is because of a staffing shortage. The book return outside stays open 24 hours."

**Warm** (the door sign, where a person reads it):
"A small change to our Saturdays: starting March 7, we'll close at 4 instead of 6 while we're short-staffed. Sorry for the shuffle — and remember, the book return by the door never sleeps, so you can drop things off anytime."

**Terse** (the text alert):
"New Saturday hours from Mar 7: close 4 p.m. (was 6). Book return open 24/7."

The levers, so you can tune it yourself: formal drops contractions and puts the institution in the subject slot ("the library will conclude"); warm adds them and puts *we* and *you* in; terse deletes everything that isn't a fact. The facts never moved. Only the relationship did.

I'm an engineer. I wrote this note for our status page: 'During the failover event, the primary node's WAL replay lag exceeded the replication threshold, triggering an automated switchover to the synchronous standby. Brief connection churn was observed.' Our customers are smart but they're accountants and office managers, not engineers. Rewrite it for them.

Here's your note with the engineering kept where it earns its place and translated where it doesn't:

"This morning our main database fell behind on copying new data to its backup — the gap grew past the safety limit we set — so the system automatically switched over to the backup, which was fully up to date. For about a minute, some connections dropped and reconnected. No data was lost."

What I kept and what I cut, so you can check my judgment:

Kept, glossed: the idea of a *safety limit* (your replication threshold) and *fully up to date* (your synchronous standby — the word "synchronous" is doing real work, because it guarantees no lost data, so I translated the guarantee instead of the mechanism).

Cut entirely: "WAL replay" and "connection churn." The first names an internal mechanism your readers can't act on; the second is jargon for something plain words say better ("dropped and reconnected").

Added: "No data was lost." Your original implies it; your readers will hunt for it. When the reader is smart but not technical, the rule is: translate mechanisms into consequences, and state the consequence they actually care about in plain words at the end.

I volunteer at my daughter's school and need to explain to third graders why we wash our hands. The health office gave me this: 'Handwashing with soap disrupts the lipid membranes of many pathogens and mechanically removes transient microorganisms from the skin surface, reducing transmission.' Can you make a version for eight-year-olds without talking down to them?

Here's the same science at reading level:

"Your hands pick up germs everywhere — from doorknobs, from the bus rail, from high-fives. Germs are tiny living things, way too small to see, and some of them can make you sick. Here's the good part: germs have a coating that's a lot like grease. Soap breaks that coating apart, the way dish soap cuts the grease on a pan. Then the water washes the broken germs off your hands and down the drain. Twenty seconds of scrubbing gives the soap time to do its job — about as long as singing 'Happy Birthday' twice."

What changed and what deliberately didn't:

Shorter sentences and concrete nouns — doorknobs and bus rails instead of "surfaces," a pan instead of "lipid membranes." But the *mechanism* is all still there: the coating, the soap breaking it, the water removing it, the time it takes. Kids don't need smaller facts; they need facts built out of things they can touch.

The condescension traps I avoided: no "boys and girls," no pretending germs are little monsters with faces, no "because grown-ups say so." The grease-on-a-pan comparison respects them — it's a real analogy to something they've actually seen in a kitchen sink.

Turn this project update into something I can send my VP. Original: 'Over the past two weeks the team has been working on the checkout redesign. We interviewed six users and built three prototype flows. Testing showed the one-page flow performed best. Engineering estimates two more weeks for the payment integration, which depends on the vendor's sandbox access, requested on the 12th and still pending. We also fixed the cart abandonment tracking bug.'

Executive version:

"Checkout redesign: on track, one external risk. Testing is done — the one-page flow won. Launch now depends on the payment vendor granting sandbox access, requested on the 12th and still pending; engineering needs two weeks once it lands. Recommend escalating the vendor request this week."

What executives actually read for is verdict, evidence, risk, ask — in that order — so that's the order I used. Your original buried all four in chronological order, which is how the work happened but not how a decision gets made.

What got cut and why: the six interviews and three prototypes became "testing is done" (the VP trusts the process happened; the *result* is the evidence). The cart-tracking bug fix vanished entirely — it's real work, but it doesn't change any decision the VP has to make, and including it dilutes the one ask in the message. What got *added*: "Recommend escalating." Your original reported the pending request as a fact. The executive version names it as the single thing leadership can do. That's the whole genre shift: a status update reports; an executive brief requests.

A customer's wedding cake order was written down for the wrong date by my bakery. We caught it and can still deliver on the right day, but the cake will be two hours later than promised. Show me the apology email in a stiff formal version and a warm version so I can see the difference.

Both versions carry the same facts and the same fix. Only the temperature changes.

**Formal:**
"Dear Ms. Alvarez, We regret to inform you that your order was recorded with an incorrect date. The error has been corrected, and your cake will be delivered on Saturday at 2:00 p.m., two hours later than originally scheduled. We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause."

**Warm:**
"Dear Ms. Alvarez — this one is on us. We wrote your date down wrong, and I'm sorry. The good news: we caught it in time. Your cake will still arrive Saturday, at 2:00 instead of noon. It will be exactly the cake you ordered. If the later time causes any problem at all with the venue, call me directly and we will sort it out."

Feel where the stiffness lives: "We regret to inform you" and "any inconvenience this may cause" are phrases that protect the writer, not the reader — "may cause" even leaves doubt that it *did* cause any. The warm version takes the blame in the first person, in the first sentence, with no padding ("this one is on us"). Then it does the thing formality can't: it gives a name and a phone number's worth of accountability — "call me directly."

For a wedding cake, send the warm one. Formal apologies are for situations where a lawyer might read them. This situation just has a bride reading it.

I docent at a maritime museum. My exhibit label reads: 'This 1892 brass binnacle housed the ship's compass and protected it from weather and iron interference aboard the coastal steamer Arden.' They want the same content as a 30-second audio guide script. How does the voice have to change?

A label is read by eyes that can go back; audio is heard once, at walking pace, by ears that can't. So the script has to slow down, point, and breathe:

"Look at the brass dome in front of you — that's a binnacle, from 1892. Inside it sat the ship's compass, the only way the steamer *Arden* knew where it was going. The brass did two jobs: it kept the sea spray off, and it shielded the compass needle from the ship's own iron, which would have pulled it off true north. Before GPS, before radar — this dome was the whole navigation system."

The specific changes: the label opens with the object; the script opens with an instruction to the eyes ("Look at...") because the listener is standing somewhere and needs orienting. Dates move from first position to mid-sentence, because ears hold facts better after they have a picture. "Iron interference" became a small story — the needle pulled off north — because audio can't use compact technical nouns; it has to unpack them as it goes. And the script ends with a scale line ("the whole navigation system") because a listener who's about to walk away needs the *why it matters* delivered, not left for a second read that will never happen.

Our HOA board wrote this notice about the new parking rule and residents are furious about the tone more than the rule: 'Pursuant to the amendment ratified 10/14, residents are hereby notified that vehicular storage on common-area asphalt surfaces is prohibited effective immediately, and violators shall be subject to enforcement action.' Rewrite it so people hear the rule without hearing a threat.

Here's the same rule in a neighbor's voice:

"A quick parking update: starting now, please don't leave stored vehicles — the ones that sit for weeks — on the shared lots. The board voted on this in October because the lots were filling up with cars that don't move, and guests and second cars had nowhere to go. If a stored vehicle is yours, you have until the end of the month to move it, and if that's a hardship, call the office and we'll work something out. Regular parked cars are fine — this is only about long-term storage."

What made the original sound like a threat: "hereby notified," "shall be subject to," "enforcement action" — that's courtroom diction, and residents hear it as the board dressing up as a government. Also notice the original never says *why*, never gives a deadline, and never distinguishes a stored car from a parked one — the three things residents actually needed.

The rewrite keeps the rule identical and equally firm ("starting now," "only about long-term storage") but adds the reason, the grace period, and the phone call. Firmness lives in clear facts. It never needed the costume.

Our app release notes are written by engineers and users say they read like a changelog for robots. This week's: 'Resolved race condition in sync engine causing duplicate entries. Deprecated legacy export endpoint. Optimized query planner for large datasets.' Make it user-voiced.

User-voiced version:

"Fixed: some of you were seeing the same note twice after syncing — that's gone. The old export tool from 2019 is being retired; the current export (Settings → Export) does everything it did. And if your library is huge, searches should feel noticeably snappier this week."

The translation rules at work: name the *symptom the user saw*, not the mechanism that caused it — nobody ever experienced a "race condition," they experienced a duplicate note. Speak in second person and past tense: "you were seeing," "that's gone." Engineer voice reports what the code did; user voice reports what changed in the user's day.

One judgment call to flag: "deprecated" became a retirement notice with a pointer to the replacement. "Deprecated" in engineer dialect means "still works, stop using it" — users read it as either nothing or panic. When a thing is going away, the user voice owes them three things the changelog omitted: what it is, when it stops, and where to go instead. I could only supply the third from your text — add the date before you publish.

The county sent us this weather statement to post at the marina office, in weather.txt. Half our boaters will read it on the board. Can you read it and give me a version that sounds like a person warning neighbors, plus tell me what you changed?

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: THE NATIONAL WEATHER SERVICE HAS ISSUED A SMALL CRAFT ADVISORY FOR COASTAL WATERS FROM MILLER POINT TO JUNEAU INLET UNTIL 1800 HOURS. WINDS 25 TO 35 KNOTS WITH GUSTS TO 45. SEAS 6 TO 9 FEET. SMALL CRAFT SHOULD EXERCISE CAUTION.

Neighbor version for the board:

"Small boats: stay in today. The weather service has an advisory up until 6 this evening — winds 25 to 35 knots, gusting to 45, with waves running 6 to 9 feet between Miller Point and Juneau Inlet. That's no weather for anything under 30 feet. If you're already out, come in early and take the inlet slow."

What I changed and why: the all-caps official voice became sentence case, because caps read as shouting at a distance and as fine print up close — either way, people skim them. "1800 hours" became "6 this evening"; your boaters think in evenings, not military time. The vague official warning "exercise caution" — which tells nobody what to *do* — became two actions: stay in, or come in early. And I led with the verdict instead of the issuing agency, because a person deciding whether to launch needs the answer in the first four words.

What I did not change: every number. Knots, gusts, wave heights, the geography, the end time — warnings are one place where the facts must survive the voice change untouched, because someone will make a safety decision off them.

My best man's toast draft starts: 'It is with great honor that I stand before you today to celebrate the union of two remarkable individuals...' My friend is a mechanic, the wedding is in a barn, and this sounds like a commencement address. Help me hear what's wrong and fix the opening.

What's wrong is register theft: the draft borrowed the voice of a ceremony *about* the couple instead of a friend *of* the couple. "It is with great honor that I stand before you" is a sentence anyone could say at any wedding — and that's the tell. Formal voice generalizes; personal voice can only belong to one room.

Try opening with the specific instead:

"The first time I met Dana, she was under the hood of my truck, telling me everything I'd done wrong to it. That was eight years ago. She's been fixing things in my life ever since — including, eventually, introducing me to the idea that my best friend could be happy. Then she introduced me to Sam, and it stopped being an idea."

The mechanics of the shift: contractions came back. Sentences got shorter and uneven — some five words, one long. The speaker appears as a person with a truck and a history instead of a function ("best man") performing an office. And the formality didn't disappear; it moved. The last sentence is genuinely ceremonious — it's just ceremonious about *these two people*, earned by the specifics before it.

Rule of thumb for toasts: if you could swap in two other names and the paragraph still works, it isn't a toast yet. It's a greeting card wearing a suit.

I run a bakery and write a monthly newsletter. A sample of my usual voice is in newsletter-sample.txt. I need a new paragraph announcing our sourdough class. Can you read my sample, figure out my voice, write the paragraph in it, and show me the match is real?

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
October notes. The ovens ran hot all month and so did we. Rye is back on Thursdays, because enough of you asked twice. If your loaf comes out pale, bring it in — we will look at it together and figure out what your kitchen did. No judgment. Your kitchen is not on trial here.

Classes are small because hands learn better than eyes. Six people, one long table, a lot of flour on the floor. You will leave with starter in a jar and dough under your nails.

Your voice, as I read it: short declarative sentences, most under twelve words, mixed with one longer rolling sentence per paragraph. Diction is kitchen-plain — ovens, flour, nails — with zero foodie vocabulary. Stance is side-by-side, not expert-above: "we will look at it together," "your kitchen is not on trial." You reassure by joking gently at the situation, never at the reader.

New paragraph, built to those specs:

"Sourdough class is back in November. Six seats, one Saturday, starter included. We will mix, stretch, and wait — sourdough makes you wait — and you will bake a loaf in our ovens before you try it in yours. If your first home loaf comes out flat, bring it in. We have all baked that loaf. It is a rite of passage, not a failure."

The audit, line by line: "Six seats, one Saturday, starter included" copies your list rhythm from "Six people, one long table." "We will mix, stretch, and wait" keeps your we-and-you partnership stance. "Bring it in" repeats your signature move — the invitation instead of the instruction. And the closer ("a rite of passage, not a failure") mirrors "not on trial here": a gentle joke whose whole job is to lower the reader's shoulders.

I drafted this email to my landlord at midnight and I'm glad I didn't send it: 'This is the THIRD time the heat has gone out and frankly it's obvious nobody cares. I pay rent on time every month, which is more than I can say for the maintenance around here. Fix it by tomorrow or I'm calling the city.' I still need the heat fixed fast. Rewrite it in a voice that gets results.

Sendable version:

"Hi Mr. Okafor — the heat went out again tonight; this is the third time this month (the 3rd and the 14th were the others). The apartment is at 58 degrees and dropping. I know you'll want to get someone in tomorrow — please let me know the window so I can be here. I've kept my rent current throughout, and I'd like us to get this one solved for good. Thanks, Daniel"

Notice: the facts got *stronger* as the temperature dropped. Your draft said "third time" in caps; the rewrite says "third time" with two dates attached — dates are harder to argue with than volume. The threat ("calling the city") became a shared goal ("get this one solved for good"), which gives him a face-saving reason to act fast instead of a reason to act defensive.

The one piece of heat I kept: "I've kept my rent current throughout." That's your leverage, and it lands harder stated flatly in a calm letter than shouted in an angry one. Anger tells the reader you're upset; calm specifics tell the reader you're *keeping records* — and people fix things faster for the tenant they believe is keeping records.
My grant draft is in grant-draft.txt. My co-writer says it 'changes personality halfway through.' Read it, find where, and unify it.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
The Harborlight Literacy Project serves 340 adults annually through volunteer-led evening classes held in donated space. Our curriculum, developed over nine years, pairs new readers with trained tutors in sessions of ninety minutes.

Anyway, the thing is, folks really love the Tuesday class — it's kind of our flagship, honestly, and the waitlist situation is getting a little wild.

Found it. The slide happens exactly at the paragraph break, and it's a full register cliff:

Paragraph one is institutional: third person, no contractions, numbers as figures ("340 adults annually"), nouns doing the work ("curriculum," "sessions"). Paragraph two is kitchen-table: "Anyway," "folks," "kind of," "a little wild" — spoken hedges and filler that belong in a conversation, plus the first contraction in the document.

This almost certainly means two people drafted it, or one person drafted tired. Either way, the funder reads the slide as carelessness, because the formal paragraph made a promise about rigor that the chatty one breaks.

Unified version, keeping paragraph one's register (grants are a formal genre — that's the right master voice here):

"The Harborlight Literacy Project serves 340 adults annually through volunteer-led evening classes held in donated space. Our curriculum, developed over nine years, pairs new readers with trained tutors in sessions of ninety minutes. The Tuesday class is our most requested offering; its waitlist has grown to 61 names, the longest in the program's history."

Note what survived the unification: the *content* of the chatty paragraph — Tuesday is popular, the waitlist is long — translated into evidence (61 names). Drift repair isn't deleting the second voice; it's translating its information into the document's chosen register.
Our clinic's style sheet is in style.txt and a draft patient letter is in letter.txt. Apply the style sheet to the letter and show me each fix against its rule.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CLINIC STYLE SHEET
1. Address the patient as "you." Never "the patient" in patient letters.
2. One idea per sentence.
3. Spell out numbers under ten.
4. No Latin abbreviations (no i.e., e.g., etc.).
5. End with a named person and a phone number, never a department.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: Dear Patient, Your lab results are in and the patient should call the office within 3 days, i.e., by Friday, to discuss them and schedule any follow-up etc. Sincerely, The Billing Department

Fixed letter:

"Dear Mrs. Chen, Your lab results are in. Please call our office by Friday — within three days — to go over them with us and schedule any follow-up you need. Sincerely, Rosa Alvarez, (555) 014-2280"

Fix by fix, against your sheet:

Rule 1 (address as "you"): "the patient should call" became "Please call" — the draft broke its own rule mid-sentence, sliding from "your results" to "the patient" as if writing about a stranger.

Rule 2 (one idea per sentence): the original was a single sentence carrying four ideas (results in, call, discuss, schedule). It is now two sentences, and the call got its own.

Rule 3 (numbers under ten spelled out): "3 days" became "three days."

Rule 4 (no Latin abbreviations): "i.e." and "etc." both deleted — "i.e., by Friday" was doing nothing anyway, since Friday simply *is* the deadline.

Rule 5 (named person, phone number): "The Billing Department" — also the wrong department for lab results — became Rosa Alvarez with a direct number.

A style sheet only works if it's checkable, and yours is: every fix above can be pointed at a numbered rule. That's what makes it a style sheet rather than a vibe.

My high school coach writes our alumni newsletter and his voice is... distinctive. Sample: 'Practice was hard. We got better. Nobody quit. That's the whole report.' I need a paragraph in his voice announcing that the gym is being renamed for him. He'd hate anything flowery.

Coach's voice, measured: average sentence length about four words. No adjectives he can't verify. Emotion expressed only through what he refuses to say. Sentiment arrives as understatement or not at all.

The announcement, in that voice:

"They're renaming the gym. It will have my name on it. I didn't ask for that. The boys and girls who played there earned it. Come in October if you can. We'll unlock the doors and look around. That's all."

Why this works in his dialect: "I didn't ask for that" is the coach's way of saying he's moved — deflection as gratitude. The credit goes to the players in one flat sentence, no decoration. And "That's all" at the end is doing the same job as his sample's "That's the whole report": it closes the door before feelings can get in, which is exactly how the reader knows the feelings are there.

The trap to avoid with a terse voice is adding warmth *to* it — one flowery sentence ("a testament to his decades of dedication") would break the spell and embarrass him in print. With minimalists, fidelity to the voice *is* the tribute.

Someone left a one-star review of my flower shop saying we 'ruined' a funeral arrangement. It wasn't our error — the funeral home gave us the wrong time — but I can't say that publicly without looking like I'm blaming them. My usual voice with customers is warm and unhurried. Help me reply without breaking it.

A reply in your voice:

"Thank you for telling us, and I'm so sorry this added pain to a hard day. The arrangement left our shop later than it should have, and whatever the reason, it was our name on the card. We've changed how we confirm times for funeral work so this can't happen the same way twice. If you're willing, I'd love to make this right with you directly — please call the shop and ask for June."

How it holds your voice under pressure: it opens with gratitude and sorrow, not defense — your first move with customers is always toward the person. The wrong-time fact is present but folded into "left our shop later than it should have" — true, sufficient, and it names no third party. "It was our name on the card" accepts the public responsibility your shop actually carries, which is the thing reviewers most want to hear and the thing defensive replies never say.

And notice the close stays unhurried: an invitation, a first name, no deadline, no "please reconsider your review" — the moment a reply asks for the rating to change, the warmth reads as strategy. This one asks for a phone call. Readers can tell the difference.

I'm a writing tutor. A student gave me a sample paragraph of her own writing and two candidate paragraphs and asked which one 'sounds like her.' Sample: 'I keep my grandmother's recipes in a shoebox, though half the cards are in a hand I can barely read anymore. Cooking from them is less about the food than about standing where she stood.' Candidates: A) 'The archive of family culinary documents represents a tangible connection to ancestral heritage and memory.' B) 'My uncle's tools hang in my garage in the order he left them. I don't fix much. Mostly I go out there to stand where he stood.' Which matches, and how do I explain it?

B, and it isn't close. Teach her to see it with three measurements:

**Sentence shape.** Her sample runs long-then-short: a winding sentence full of subordinate clauses, then a clean landing. B does exactly that — two medium sentences, then the short fall of "I don't fix much," then the long close. A is one uniform block of a sentence; it has no rhythm in common with her at all.

**Diction level.** She writes in objects: shoebox, cards, a hand. B writes in objects: tools, garage, order. A writes in abstractions: "archive," "culinary documents," "ancestral heritage" — words no one can touch.

**The signature move.** Her sample ends by echoing its own image: "standing where she stood." B ends with the same gesture — "stand where he stood" — which is her voice's fingerprint: a physical position standing in for grief. A has no gesture; it has a thesis.

The lesson worth giving her: voice isn't vocabulary size or correctness. It's the pattern of choices you'd make again without thinking — sentence rhythm, concrete-over-abstract, and the one move that's yours. B makes all three of her choices. A makes none of them, and is, by the usual measures, the 'better' writing. That's the interesting part.

I'm the founder of a small tutoring company. My draft of our 'about' letter keeps coming out corporate: 'Founded in 2019, Brightpath Tutoring leverages a network of certified educators to deliver measurable outcomes for learners across the tri-county area.' I hate it. It's me and six tutors. Help.

The problem isn't polish — it's that the draft is written in the voice of a company a hundred times your size, and readers can hear the costume. Here's the same information at your actual size:

"I started Brightpath in 2019, tutoring at kitchen tables. There are seven of us now — me and six tutors I hired because I'd want them teaching my own kids. We work across the tri-county area, and we keep our groups small enough that we know every student's name, school, and the exact chapter where math started going sideways."

Changes that matter: "leverages a network of certified educators" became "six tutors I hired because..." — the corporate version hides the founder; the personal version makes her the guarantee. "Measurable outcomes" became a specific, checkable claim (we know where math went sideways), which is more credible than any outcome-word. And "learners" became "students" — "learners" is a word only institutions use; people have students, children, kids.

A useful test for founder letters: read it aloud and ask, *would I say this to a parent at a school fair?* Every sentence that fails that test is the costume. Cut it, and what's left is usually the company.

I manage a small team. My director asked me to 'just forward my summary up the chain in your own words,' and I realized my draft sounds exactly like her — all her phrases, her sentence patterns. Is that a problem? Show me what voice borrowing looks like and how to get mine back.

It's a real phenomenon and worth catching. Voice borrowing usually looks like this — a manager's summary written in the director's dialect:

Borrowed: "Going forward, we'll leverage the onboarding learnings to drive synergy across the Q3 deliverables and circle back on bandwidth."

The borrower's own voice, same content: "The new onboarding worked. We're using the same approach for the fall hires, and I'll know by September whether we need one more person."

Why it happens: we absorb the voice of whoever evaluates us, the way you pick up an accent living somewhere. It isn't dishonest, but it costs you two things. First, precision — borrowed phrases are usually vague ("leverage," "synergy," "circle back") because they were designed for a level of the company where vagueness is safer. Second, credit — a summary that sounds like your director makes your judgment invisible; the reader can't tell where her thinking ends and yours begins.

The fix isn't a different style guide; it's a translation habit. Draft however it comes out, then do one pass asking of every sentence: *what do I actually know, and how would I say it to a colleague I trust?* "Drive synergy across deliverables" rarely survives that question. "We're using the same approach for the fall hires" does, because it's yours.

I have a paragraph of my grandfather's writing and I want to derive a style sheet from it so the family can keep his voice in the reunion cookbook. His paragraph: 'We ate at six. Always six. Mother rang the bell whether the soup was ready or not, and we came, because the bell was not a suggestion. You did not complain about food in that house. You ate it, and you said thank you, and if you were wise you asked for seconds before the gravy boat made its second round.' Derive the rules.

Five rules, each with its evidence:

**1. Short sentences, and shorter ones for emphasis.** "We ate at six. Always six." The fragment after the full sentence is the punch — he shortens to land a point. Cookbook entries in his voice should average under fifteen words a sentence, with fragments allowed only for emphasis.

**2. Rules of the house stated as facts of nature.** "The bell was not a suggestion." He never writes "I think" or "we believed" — custom is described as physics. State family customs the same way: as how the world was, not as opinions.

**3. Second person for instruction.** "You did not complain... You ate it, and you said thank you." When he teaches, the reader stands in the child's chair. Recipe notes should use *you*, present tense, no hedging.

**4. Humor is dry and comes last in the sentence.** "...if you were wise you asked for seconds before the gravy boat made its second round." The joke rides at the end of a serious sentence, never announced. No exclamation points anywhere — that's the corollary.

**5. Concrete objects carry the memory.** Bell, soup, gravy boat. He never writes "mealtimes were special." If a cookbook note drifts into abstraction ("food brought us together"), this rule sends it back for an object.

A style sheet derived this way is checkable: any family member can hold a draft against the five rules and point. That's what keeps a voice alive after its owner can't edit anymore — not imitation, but rules with evidence.

I'm writing to my neighborhood listserv trying to convince skeptical homeowners that rooftop solar pencils out. My draft leads with how much I love my panels. They're... not convinced by my enthusiasm. Restructure it.

Skeptics don't need your enthusiasm — they need their own objection answered before your argument starts. Your draft leads with the thing they're discounting. Lead with the objection instead:

"The fair question is whether the panels ever actually pay for themselves, so here are my real numbers, not the brochure's. Our system cost $18,400 after the credit. Our electric bill averaged $212 a month before; last year it averaged $31. That's $2,172 a year, which puts payback in year nine of a 25-year warranty. The risk is real too: if we moved in year five, we'd lose money. We aren't moving. Your math will differ — shade, roof angle, and your rate all move it — and I'll happily share my bills with anyone who wants to run theirs."

What changed structurally: the strongest counterargument ("these never pay off") is now the first sentence, stated fairly, in their voice. Then numbers — *your* numbers, with the source named (real bills, not the installer). Then the honest risk, conceded before they raise it, which is what makes the rest believable. Enthusiasm appears nowhere, and the letter is more persuasive for it: a skeptic trusts a writer who volunteers the weak point of their own case.

My update to the school board is in board-update.txt. Board members read forty of these the night before the meeting. Mine is one long paragraph. Read it and restructure it so the key point is findable in five seconds.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: This semester the reading program expanded to all six elementary schools and served 1,140 students, up from 720 last year, and volunteer hours rose to 3,900, while the per-student cost fell from $86 to $61 because the district absorbed the coordinator salary, and we are requesting that the board renew the program for two years and increase the materials budget from $12,000 to $15,500 to cover the added schools, with the full breakdown attached in Appendix B.

Restructured:

**Request: renew the reading program for two years and raise the materials budget from $12,000 to $15,500.**

Why: the program now serves 1,140 students (up from 720) in all six elementary schools. Per-student cost *fell* from $86 to $61 because the district absorbed the coordinator's salary. Volunteers contributed 3,900 hours. Full breakdown: Appendix B.

Your original contained every fact — and hid all of them equally. A single paragraph with five numbers and the request in the middle is a wall: a tired board member skimming at 10 p.m. finds nothing to hold. The restructure does three things. The ask goes first, bolded, in the exact form they'll vote on. The evidence follows in descending order of persuasiveness (more kids, *lower* unit cost, free labor). And the appendix is pointed to rather than summarized, which respects the five-second reader and the thorough one at once.

The rule for busy readers: they don't read less carefully, they read in a different order — verdict, evidence, detail. Write in the order they read.

I run a small catering company. A client booked us for a family gathering, and two days before, her father died. The gathering is now after the funeral. I need to email her about rescheduling the menu tasting. I keep writing it too cheerful or too stiff. Help me find the register.

The register you're looking for is plain and warm: short sentences, no brightness, business handled so gently it almost disappears.

"Dear Mrs. Osei, I was very sorry to hear about your father. Please don't give the tasting a thought — we'll hold everything as it is, and when you're ready, we'll pick a new time that suits your family. There's no charge for the change and no hurry at all. We're here when you need us. — Priya, Harbor & Vine Catering"

Why each choice: "I was very sorry to hear" is the standard phrase, and standard is right here — originality in condolence feels like performance. The business content is reduced to pure reassurance: nothing is lost, nothing costs, nothing is urgent. Notice what's absent: no "celebration of life" reframing (that's hers to say, not yours), no exclamation points, no "silver lining." And the signature is a person, not the company — grief is addressed person to person.

The stiff versions fail by hiding behind the company; the cheerful ones fail by asking her to match your energy. This one asks nothing of her at all. That's the whole register: a message that makes no demands.

I'm a lab tech writing a note to the principal investigator about an experiment. Everything came out as expected except one assay. My draft hedges everything equally: 'The results may possibly suggest that the treatment might have had some effect in certain conditions.' She will check every claim. Fix my hedging.

Your draft hedges everything at the same strength, which tells an expert reader nothing — a hedge is information, and uniform hedging is noise. Place each hedge exactly where the uncertainty actually is:

"The treatment reduced marker A by 31% across all four replicates (p = 0.004). Marker B moved in the same direction but did not reach significance; with four replicates I can't separate a small real effect from noise. The C assay failed outright — the control degraded — so I have no reading on C at all. My read: the effect on A is solid, B is worth a powered follow-up, and C needs a rerun before it says anything."

The calibration, claim by claim: A gets no hedge at all, because the data is strong and an expert will *distrust* a hedge there — it reads as if you're hiding a weakness. B gets a hedge with a *reason attached* (replicate count), which is the difference between caution and vagueness. C gets the strongest statement in the note — a flat admission of no data — because for a checking reader, "the assay failed" is more valuable than any result.

Expert readers don't want confidence or caution in general. They want to be able to rebuild your uncertainty map from your sentences. Hedge like a surveyor, not like a fog machine.

Half my warehouse crew are strong readers of Spanish and working on English. Our new-hire instructions are full of idioms I didn't even notice: 'Hit the ground running on your first shift. Don't sweat the small stuff — ask your lead, they've been around the block. Keep your eyes peeled for the blue bins; that's where the ball gets rolling. We'll touch base Friday.' Clean it up without making it sound like a children's book.

Cleaned version, same friendly tone, zero idioms:

"Start working at a normal pace on your first shift — nobody expects speed yet. Small questions are welcome. Ask your lead; they have done this job for years. Watch carefully for the blue bins; every order starts there. We will meet briefly on Friday to check how your first week went."

The idioms I found and what each became: "hit the ground running" → "start working at a normal pace" (and notice the original actually *contradicts* what you want — running is the last thing a new hire should do). "Don't sweat the small stuff" → "small questions are welcome": the idiom says *ignore* small things, but your real meaning was *ask about* them, so the rewrite is more accurate, not just plainer. "Been around the block" → "done this job for years." "Keep your eyes peeled" → "watch carefully." "Where the ball gets rolling" → "where every order starts." "Touch base" → "meet briefly."

Why it doesn't sound like a children's book: the sentences stay adult in length and content — what changed is that every word now means what it literally says. Idioms are compression for native speakers and riddles for everyone else. Plain phrasing isn't dumbing down; it's un-encrypting.

I'm writing a letter to the editor opposing a rezoning on my street. Readers of the paper mostly support it — they see housing, I see my street's water pressure and parking. If I just vent, they'll dismiss me. How do I write for readers who start out against me?

Write the letter that grants their case first — fully, fairly, in its strongest form — and then shows the one fact it doesn't cover:

"The case for the rezoning is a good one, and I share it: this city needs more homes, and building near the bus line is the right place for them. If the question were only housing, I'd sign the petition myself. The question the council hasn't answered is narrower. Our street's water main was laid in 1954 for forty houses. The development adds ninety homes to that main, and the city's own engineering memo — page 6 — says the pressure study hasn't been done. I'm not asking the council to choose between housing and my street. I'm asking it to do the study first, and zone second. If the main can carry it, I'll help welcome the new neighbors."

Why this structure works on a hostile reader: the opening agreement disarms the dismissal reflex — you can't be waved off as anti-housing when you've made the housing case better than its supporters did. The opposition then shrinks to one verifiable, checkable fact (an undone study, cited to a page), which moves the argument from values to homework. And the closing conditional ("if the main can carry it...") gives persuadable readers a way to agree with you without admitting they were wrong — they only have to agree that studies should come before votes. Persuasion of skeptics is mostly architecture: shared ground first, one narrow claim, an exit ramp.

Our team meeting notes are a transcript-like blob. My manager wants a decision memo instead. Notes say: 'Talked about the vendor switch. Maria had concerns about migration time. Dev said staging is ready. Some discussion of cost — the new vendor is cheaper per seat but onboarding is $4k. Decided to switch starting October, Maria to own the migration plan by next Friday. Also postponed the offsite.' Turn it into the memo.

Decision memo:

**Decided:** We switch to the new vendor starting in October. Maria owns the migration plan, due next Friday.

**Why:** Cheaper per seat; staging environment is ready. Onboarding costs $4,000 one-time — accepted as part of the switch.

**Open concern:** Migration time (Maria). Her plan, due Friday, is where this gets resolved.

**Deferred:** Team offsite — postponed, no new date.

The transformation isn't summarization; it's *sorting by consequence*. A transcript preserves the order things were said; a memo preserves only what changes someone's obligations. Notice what happened to each element: the decision and its owner moved to the top because two people now have deadlines. Maria's concern wasn't deleted — it was reclassified from "discussion" to "open concern" and attached to the deliverable that answers it, which is where concerns do work instead of evaporating. The cost discussion compressed to the one number that was actually weighed. And the offsite, which nobody decided anything about, got one honest line instead of the paragraph of chat it occupied in the room.

Test for any memo: could a person who missed the meeting act correctly from this alone? The blob fails that test; four short sections pass it.

I'm reviewing a junior engineer's pull request. The change works, but there's a caching approach I'm not sure about — it might break under load, or might be fine; I genuinely don't know. My comment draft says: 'This is wrong and will cause problems.' That's not fair, but 'looks good!' isn't honest either. Help me write the comment an expert would write.

The comment calibrated to what you actually know:

"This works, and the tests prove the happy path well. The part I can't verify — and I want to be precise that this is my uncertainty, not a found bug — is the cache under concurrent writes. If two requests update the same key together, I *believe* the second write can be lost, but I haven't constructed the case. Two ways forward, your pick: add a test that forces that interleaving, or add a comment marking this as the known soft spot so the next person finds it flagged. Either way, I'm approving — this is a 'show me or label it,' not a block."

The anatomy, for a reader who will check: observation separated from inference ("works, tests prove it" vs. "I believe the second write can be lost"). The uncertainty is *owned* — "my uncertainty, not a found bug" — which protects the junior from chasing a ghost and protects you from crying wolf. The request is made checkable: a test that forces the case either exists or it doesn't. And the stakes are stated plainly at the end (approve, not block), because in review comments the most misread thing is severity.

The original draft — "this is wrong and will cause problems" — claimed a certainty you don't have. Expert voice isn't firmer than the evidence; it's *exactly* as firm as the evidence, with the seams showing.
The safety notice in notice.txt goes on the break-room wall. A third of our staff read English as a second language. Read it and give me a version with the idioms taken out.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: NOTICE: When in doubt, err on the side of caution around the baler. Keep the area shipshape — a spill left sitting is an accident waiting to happen. If the guard is on the fritz, don't try to be a hero: lock it out and call maintenance, day or night. Cutting corners here costs more than time.

Plain version for the wall:

"NOTICE: If you are not sure the baler is safe, do not use it. Keep the area clean and dry — a spill on the floor can cause a fall. If the safety guard is broken, do not try to fix it yourself. Turn the machine off, lock it, and call maintenance. You can call at any time, day or night. Doing this work the fast, unsafe way can cause a serious injury."

Idiom by idiom: "err on the side of caution" → "if you are not sure it is safe, do not use it" — the idiom describes an attitude; the rewrite gives an action, which is what a safety notice is for. "Shipshape" → "clean and dry," with the reason added because "an accident waiting to happen" named no accident; the actual one is a fall. "On the fritz" → "broken." "Don't be a hero" → "do not try to fix it yourself" — "hero" is sarcasm in the original, and sarcasm is the first thing that fails across languages. "Cutting corners" → "the fast, unsafe way."

One thing I preserved on purpose: "day or night" survived, because it's literal — it means exactly what it says in every dialect of English. The test isn't whether a phrase is colorful; it's whether a reader can decode it from the words alone.

I write our elementary school's newsletter. One paragraph has to serve parents (who want warmth and clarity) and the district office (which reads it for compliance — every event needs a date, a cost, and a permission note). Show me a paragraph that serves both without sounding like two documents stapled together.

One paragraph, two readers, no staples:

"Our third graders are heading to the tide pools at Miller's Cove on Friday, May 8 — they'll be hunting for hermit crabs and sea stars with Ms. Okafor's class guide in hand. The trip is free for families; the PTA is covering the buses. Permission slips went home in Tuesday folders and need to come back signed by Monday, May 4. Wear boots that can get wet — the rocks are slippery and the crabs are worth it."

How the double duty works: the district's three required facts (date: May 8; cost: free, buses covered; permission: slips back by May 4) are all present and checkable — but each one is carried inside a sentence that also does warmth work. The deadline sentence is pure logistics, so it's wrapped between hermit crabs and wet boots, the two sentences a parent actually reads. Compliance buried in the middle of a paragraph gets read; compliance in its own paragraph gets skimmed by parents and warmth in its own paragraph gets flagged by districts.

The failure mode to avoid is the stapled version — three warm sentences, then a block of bolded requirements — because each audience learns to skip the other's half, and the parents skip the half with the deadline in it. Weave, don't stack.

I left this note on the fridge for my roommate: 'Interesting how the dishes somehow wash themselves when I do them. No rush though — they've only been in the sink since Tuesday!!' I know. Rewrite it so it says what I actually mean.

What you actually mean, said directly:

"Hey — the dishes from Tuesday are still in the sink, and I washed the last two loads. Can you take this one tonight? If we alternate, it stops being a thing. — J"

The barbs in the original, so you can recognize your own aim next time: "somehow wash themselves" is sarcasm doing the work of a fact (I did them). "No rush though" is a false permission — you say the opposite of what you mean and dare them to notice. And "since Tuesday!!" is a timestamp delivered as an accusation instead of information.

The direct version keeps every real fact — Tuesday, the two loads, the sink — and converts each barb into either a fact or a request. Notice it also adds the thing passive-aggressive notes never include: a proposal ("if we alternate"). The sarcastic note wants the roommate to *feel* something; the direct one wants the dishes washed and the pattern changed. It also has a better success rate, because a person can comply with a request. They can only resent a barb.

I owe a client an email because their report is two days late. My draft: 'I am so, so sorry, this is completely unacceptable of me, I feel terrible, you've been so patient and I don't deserve it, I completely dropped the ball and I promise I'm beating myself up about it, the report will be there Friday and again I am SO sorry.' Help.

One apology, full strength, then business:

"I'm sorry — your report is two days late, and that's on me. It will be in your inbox Friday by noon. I've moved my review step earlier in the week so this doesn't repeat. Thank you for your patience with us."

What got cut and why: your draft apologizes five times, and each repetition *weakens* the one before it — by the third "sorry," a client stops hearing remorse and starts hearing a person who needs comforting, which reverses who owes whom. "I don't deserve it" and "I'm beating myself up" ask the client to manage your feelings on top of waiting for their report.

What replaced the groveling: a specific new time (Friday by noon — a promise that can be kept or broken, which is what makes it an actual commitment) and one sentence about the fix. Clients don't measure apologies in volume; they measure them in whether the next deadline moves. Apologize once, precisely, then spend the rest of the email proving it with logistics.

I got promoted and have to post an update to the team channel. My draft: 'Thrilled and humbled to announce that after crushing every target this year and basically rebuilding our onboarding from scratch (you're welcome!), I've been promoted to Senior Manager. Big things ahead — watch this space!' My manager said 'maybe tone it down.' She's right, isn't she.

She is. The quiet version:

"Some news: I've been promoted to Senior Manager, effective next month. Thank you to everyone who worked with me on the onboarding rebuild this year — that project is a big part of why this happened, and it was a team effort in the real sense. My focus stays the same: onboarding and the two launches this fall. My door's open as always."

What was removed: "crushing every target" and "basically rebuilt from scratch" — claims your teammates will silently fact-check, and several of them were *in* that rebuild. "You're welcome" is the worst phrase in the genre: it bills people for a gift. And "watch this space" promises a spectacle nobody asked for.

What stayed: the fact, the date, the genuine credit (made believable by the admission that it's "a big part" of the reason, not all of it), and continuity — "my focus stays the same" — which is the sentence your team actually needs, because a promotion announcement is, for everyone else, a change announcement. Confidence reads as quiet because it doesn't need the reader to agree it's impressive. The facts, stated plainly, do the impressing on their own schedule.

Our studio's welcome email to new clients is technically fine but reads like a parking ticket: 'Your booking is confirmed for Tuesday at 10:00. Arrive 10 minutes early. Late arrivals may be rescheduled. Payment is due at the time of service.' I don't want it gushy. Just... less cold. Two degrees warmer.

Two degrees, no gush:

"You're booked for Tuesday at 10:00 — we're glad to have you. Try to arrive about 10 minutes early so we can start on time and you get your full session. Running late? Call us and we'll do our best to fit you in. Payment is due at your visit."

Count the changes, because they're all small: "Your booking is confirmed" became "You're booked" plus four warm words ("we're glad to have you") — one clause, not a paragraph of delight. "Arrive 10 minutes early" gained a reason ("so you get your full session") — coldness often isn't tone at all, it's unexplained demands; a reason converts an order into a courtesy. "Late arrivals may be rescheduled" — the threat — became an invitation to call, with the honest limit kept ("we'll do our best" promises effort, not miracles). "Payment is due at the time of service" softened only to "at your visit."

That's the lesson of the two-degree warm-up: warmth is almost never adjectives. It's small words — *we're glad*, *try*, *call us* — and reasons given where orders stood.

I wrote the announcement for our warehouse's new safety-training requirement and tried to make it fun: 'Good news, party people! Everyone's favorite topic — safety training — is back! Four hours of thrills, spills (the kind we prevent!), and a quiz at the end that you'll just love. Don't be the one who skips — Gary in Accounting still hasn't lived down the forklift video incident.' My supervisor killed it. Why, and what's the version that survives?

Your supervisor is right, and it's worth knowing exactly why, because the jokes aren't bad — the *occasion* is wrong. Safety training exists because people get hurt; a comic frame tells staff the company doesn't quite believe that. And one joke has a specific victim: Gary is now the permanent punchline of a mandatory announcement, which is a small cruelty with an official letterhead.

The surviving version:

"Safety training is scheduled for all warehouse staff during the weeks of May 12 and May 19. Sessions run four hours and end with a short quiz. Your lead has your session time. This year's training covers two incidents from our own floor last year — both ended without serious injury, and both were preventable. The goal is that they stay the last two."

What was lost, honestly: your draft had energy, and this one won't make anyone smile on the way to the session. That loss is real, and it's the price. What was gained: the last two sentences give the training a *reason rooted in your own building*, which motivates better than comedy ever did — people lean in for "this happened here" in a way they never lean in for jokes.

Humor in workplace writing is a spice with a contraindication list: never on safety, never on someone else's misfortune, never from the institution downward. Your instincts about livening up dull announcements are good — aim them at the picnic, the holiday schedule, the softball team.
There's an email in kitchen-email.txt that I sent to a coworker about the shared office kitchen. Reading it back, it's... pointed. Read it and rewrite it as the direct version I should have sent.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
Subject: Kitchen :)
Hi all! Just a friendly reminder that some of us have been heroically cleaning up lunches that aren't ours. Per my last email, the fridge is not a storage unit for science projects. If everyone could just try to remember that other people use this space too, that would be amazing. Thanks so much!!

The direct version:

"Subject: Kitchen — Friday cleanout starts this week
Hi everyone — I've cleaned up other people's lunches from the shared fridge three times this month, and I'm going to stop doing that. Starting this Friday, anything unlabelled goes in the bin at 4 p.m. Label your food with your name and the date and it's safe. If the fridge is genuinely too small, tell me and I'll raise it with office management. — Sam"

The barbs in your original, named: "heroically" (sarcasm), "per my last email" (the classic corporate dagger — it says *you didn't listen*), "science projects" (mockery of unnamed people who will all assume it's them), "that would be amazing" and the smiley subject line (sweetness used as a wrapper so the sender can deny the sting). Every one of those lets the writer feel honest while staying deniable.

The direct version trades deniability for results: it states the writer's own behavior change ("I'm going to stop"), a rule with a time (Friday, 4 p.m.), a way to comply (label it), and a genuine offer at the end. People can't follow a hint. They can follow a rule — and most of them, given a clear one, will.

I can't go to my cousin's recital and my draft text is a paragraph of apologies: 'I am SO sorry, I feel awful, work is insane, you know I'd be there if I could, please don't be mad, I'm the worst cousin, I'll make it up to you I swear, sorry sorry.' Fix it.

Fixed:

"I can't make the recital Saturday — work has me in the office all weekend, and I'm sorry to miss it. I know you've been practicing for months. Will someone record your piece? I want to hear the Chopin properly, not through a phone speaker if I can help it. Break a leg. — R"

One apology ("I'm sorry to miss it"), stated once at full value. Everything your draft spent on self-punishment — "I'm the worst cousin," the triple sorry — got replaced with evidence that you actually care about the *recital*: you know it's Saturday, you know she's practiced for months, you know it's Chopin, and you want the good recording. That specificity is worth more than any volume of guilt, because guilt is about the sender and attention is about the receiver.

Notice also what the direct version does with the reason: one clause ("work has me in the office all weekend"), no saga. A short reason reads as true; a long defense reads as a case being built. Decline cleanly, show you know what you're missing, ask for the recording. That's the whole shape.

For a grant application I need a short bio. My draft: 'Dr. Ines Halvorsen is an internationally recognized leader in coastal ecology whose groundbreaking research has transformed our understanding of salt marsh restoration, earning her numerous accolades and the admiration of colleagues worldwide.' The funder is a small regional foundation. Even I can hear it. Rewrite.

Quiet version:

"Dr. Ines Halvorsen studies how salt marshes recover after restoration. Over fifteen years she has led marsh projects at nine sites along the Gulf Coast, including the Bayou Terrebonne marsh, which now supports nesting birds for the first time in four decades. Her group's planting methods are used by three state agencies. She teaches ecology at the University of Louisiana and still runs the volunteer planting days herself."

The trumpet phrases and their replacements: "internationally recognized leader" → the work's actual footprint (nine sites, three agencies using the methods) — a regional funder can't verify "internationally recognized" and doesn't need it; they can verify a marsh. "Groundbreaking" and "transformed our understanding" → one concrete, checkable outcome (nesting birds, first time in forty years), which persuades precisely because it can be falsified. "Numerous accolades" → deleted entirely; awards lists in bios read as compensation.

The sentence I added — "still runs the volunteer planting days herself" — does more for a small foundation than every superlative in your draft, because regional funders fund people they'll meet. Confidence, in a bio, is the willingness to let countable facts carry the impressiveness.

Our dance studio sends a payment reminder that reads: 'Your account is past due. Remit payment immediately to avoid interruption of services. Failure to comply will result in suspension.' Parents find it scary and it sounds like a utility shutoff notice. We do need to be paid, though. Warmer, but still a reminder.

Warmer, still unmistakably a reminder:

"Hi Dana — a quick note that October's tuition ($85) hasn't come through yet. It happens! Cards expire and autopay hiccups. You can update your card in the portal, or bring payment to the front desk this week. If something's changed for your family, talk to us — we'd much rather make a plan than lose Mia from class. — Front desk, Riverbend Dance"

What softened: the legal threats ("remit," "failure to comply," "suspension") — vocabulary borrowed from debt collection, aimed at parents who mostly forgot. What *didn't* soften: the amount, the month, the deadline ("this week"), and the fact of a consequence, rephrased as relationship ("we'd rather make a plan than lose Mia") rather than punishment. A reminder can be warm without being vague; vagueness is what actually costs you money, because a vague reminder is an ignorable one.

The highest-value addition is "It happens! Cards expire and autopay hiccups." Most late payers are embarrassed, and embarrassment causes avoidance. Giving them a face-saving, *true* explanation — most of your late payments really are expired cards — gets more bills paid than any threat in the original.

Our CEO wrote a draft message to staff about the layoffs next month and tried to soften it with humor: 'Well, folks, the rumor mill got this one right for once! We're doing a little spring cleaning on the org chart. Some of you will be starting exciting new chapters elsewhere!' HR flagged it. I need to explain to him why it can't go out and give him the version that can.

Why it can't go out, in one sentence you can say to him: every joke in the draft is at the expense of the people losing their jobs, told by the person who isn't. "Spring cleaning" compares employees to clutter. "Exciting new chapters" — the phrase layoff communications always reach for — asks frightened people to perform gratitude. And "the rumor mill got this one right" opens by confirming that leadership let rumors carry the news first. Humor softens messages only when the joker shares the risk; here the risk is entirely the audience's.

The version that can go out:

"I am writing with difficult news. Next month we will eliminate 24 positions, about 8 percent of the company. If your role is affected, you will hear it from your manager in person this week, not by email or rumor. Affected employees receive three months of severance and six months of continued health coverage, and our HR team will work with each person individually. I made this decision, and I won't dress it up: the company took on costs the revenue doesn't support. I'm sorry to those who will bear the cost of that."

What's in it: the number, the share, the timeline, the terms, and ownership — "I made this decision" — with the cause stated in one honest clause. No warmth is performed and none is needed; at this temperature, respect *is* clarity plus terms plus accountability. Save his humor for the all-hands where he's the one on the hook.

Something is dull about this paragraph from our community workshop's flyer but I can't say what: 'The workshop on Alder Street opens its doors at nine. Twelve benches line the walls beneath the tall windows. A kettle waits on the counter beside the tea tin. Sign-up sheets for spring fill quickly by Wednesday noon.' Diagnose it with actual evidence, not vibes.

The evidence is countable. Here are the sentence lengths, in words: 10, 9, 10, 9. Four sentences, two lengths, alternating like a metronome. Nothing is wrong with any single sentence — the paragraph is dull because the *rhythm* never varies, so the reader's ear stops listening even while the eyes keep going. Monotony in prose is usually this: not repeated words, but repeated lengths.

Same facts, rhythm broken:

"The workshop opens at nine. By ten, all twelve benches are taken, the kettle has boiled twice, and somebody has already sawed a board to the wrong length and laughed about it. Tea at eleven. Then the real work starts."

New lengths: 5, 27, 3, 5. The long sentence now has somewhere to *be* long against, and the three-word sentence ("Tea at eleven") lands like a bell. Notice I didn't add information — the wrong-length board was implied by any real workshop — I added *contrast*.

The diagnostic habit to keep: when a paragraph feels flat, count the sentence lengths before touching a word. If they cluster within a few words of each other, you don't have a wording problem. You have a rhythm problem, and the fix is surgery on lengths, not synonyms.

I wrote instructions for volunteers at our seed library and reading them aloud I keep tripping: 'Sort the seeds by size, set aside the split seeds, and seal the sorted seeds in the small sacks. Sister Sue's seed-sorting system succeeds.' I sound ridiculous. Smooth it out.

The tongue-twister effect comes from the same consonant cluster — the s/sh sounds — landing in nearly every word, plus one sentence ("Sister Sue's...") that is pure alliteration. Aloud, your tongue has to reset for each one. Smoothed:

"Divide the seeds into piles by size. Put any cracked or broken ones in the tray on the left. Then pack the good seeds into the small paper bags and close each one with a fold. This is the method Sue worked out last spring, and it works well."

What changed mechanically: the s-heavy verbs got spread out — "sort" stayed once, "set aside" became "put," "seal" became "pack" and "close with a fold." The information is identical (three steps, same order, same tray), but no two steps in a row now start with the same mouth shape. And Sue keeps her credit — "the method Sue worked out" — without her name becoming a tongue obstacle.

The general test is the one you already used: read it aloud, at the speed a tired volunteer would. Written prose can hide clusters that spoken prose can't. Any text that will be *heard* — instructions, scripts, announcements — has to pass the mouth, not just the eye.

My fundraising sentence is: 'With your help, we can give every kid in the county a library card this summer.' It's fine, I guess, but it doesn't land. A friend said the important word is in the wrong place. Show me what she means.

Your friend is pointing at the end of the sentence. Readers remember the last word the way they remember the last note of a song — it's where emphasis naturally falls — and your sentence ends on "this summer," a detail. The important word is "every."

Watch it move:

"This summer, with your help, we can give a library card to every kid in the county."

Now the sentence builds through the logistics (when, how) and lands on the *scope* — every kid — which is the actual emotional claim of your campaign. "Every" in final position gets a tiny spotlight: the reader's inner voice stresses it without being told.

Two more versions to feel the lever: end on "library card" ("...we can put a library card in the hands of every kid in the county this summer" — no; that ends on "summer" again). End on the county: "...a library card for every kid — every single one in the county." That one trades smoothness for insistence.

The working rule: find the word you'd underline if you read the sentence aloud, and rebuild the sentence so that word comes last. If you can't tell which word it is, the sentence doesn't know what it's about yet — and no rearrangement will save it until you decide.

My packing list for new movers (I run a moving company) reads weird and I don't know why: 'You should pack the kitchen first. Bedding in the big boxes. Don't forget labeling every box on two sides. The truck gets loaded by our crew.' What's wrong with it as a list?

Each item is built from a different grammatical part, so the list stutters — item one is a command to *you*, item two is a fragment about bedding, item three is a warning, item four changes the subject to the crew. The reader has to re-parse every line. Repaired, with every item as the same shape — a plain instruction in the same voice:

"Pack the kitchen first. Put bedding in the big boxes. Label every box on two sides. Leave the truck loading to our crew."

Four items, four imperative verbs in the same form (pack, put, label, leave), each one line, each doing one job. That's parallel structure: not elegance, but a rhythm the reader can predict, so their attention stays on the content instead of the grammar.

A quick way to check any list: read only the first two words of each item in a column. If the shapes jump around — "You should / Bedding in / Don't forget / The truck" — the list isn't parallel. If they march — "Pack the / Put bedding / Label every / Leave the" — it is.

Here's a sentence from my trail-guide draft that got away from me: 'The trail climbs past the falls and the old mill and the ridge opens up and you can see the whole valley and the river bending through it and the town beyond with the church spire and the fields going gold in the late light and it's the best view in the county.' I like the rush of it but readers say they get lost. Repunctuate without killing it.

The rush is worth keeping — it's the feeling of the view opening — but a reader needs two or three places to breathe. Punctuation is how you give them air without slowing the climb:

"The trail climbs past the falls and the old mill, and then the ridge opens up: the whole valley, the river bending through it, the town beyond with its church spire, the fields going gold in the late light. The best view in the county."

What the punctuation is doing: the comma after "mill" separates the climb from the reveal. The colon is the hinge of the whole sentence — everything before it is effort, everything after it is the payoff, and a colon tells the reader *here it comes*. The list of sights runs on commas only, no "ands," so it reads as one sweeping glance instead of a checklist. And "The best view in the county" became a fragment on purpose: after the long exhale of the view, the short verdict lands harder alone than it ever did trailing an "and it's."

The principle: a run-on isn't fixed by chopping it into equal pieces. It's fixed by punctuation that marks the *shape* of the experience — effort, reveal, verdict — so the reader's breath follows the hiker's.

Opposite problem from most people: my draft about our lighthouse tour is all short sentences and it reads like a telegram. 'The light was built in 1873. It stands ninety feet tall. Ships used it until 1962. The keeper lived in the cottage. His family stayed through the winters. You can climb the tower today.' Make it breathe without losing clarity.

Choppiness is the mirror of the run-on: every sentence the same short length, each fact in its own box, no sentence allowed to lean on the next. The fix is joining where the ideas are already joined:

"The light was built in 1873 and stands ninety feet tall. Ships steered by it until 1962, while the keeper and his family lived in the cottage below and stayed through winters that cut the point off from the town for weeks. You can climb the tower today."

What merged and why: the two facts about the tower (built, height) became one sentence because they're one subject. The ships, the keeper, and the winters became a single long sentence because they're one *story* — the working life of the place — and the long sentence is allowed to accumulate the way the years did. "You can climb the tower today" stayed short and separate on purpose: after the long historical breath, a short present-tense sentence works like a door opening.

The clarity survived because joining sentences doesn't blur facts when the joints are honest ("and," "while") — each fact is still checkable. What's gone is only the telegram rhythm. Rule of thumb: short sentences are a spice. A paragraph of nothing else tastes like a list of headlines.

Our ad copy for a bakery delivery service came out as: 'Fresh-baked bread, brought briskly to your breakfast table by our bright-eyed bakers — the best bite in the borough!' The owner loves it. Our test readers said it was 'a lot.' Adjudicate.

Your test readers are right, and here's the precise reason: the sentence has two sound systems running at once. The b-alliteration (bread, briskly, breakfast, bright-eyed, bakers, best, bite, borough — eight b's) is a drumbeat, and the meaning has to shout over it. One or two alliterating words charm; eight make the reader hear the *writing* instead of the bread.

Trimmed to keep the owner's music at half volume:

"Fresh-baked bread, delivered to your table before breakfast. Our bakers start at three in the morning so you don't have to."

What's left of the original music: "fresh-baked bread" and "before breakfast" still chime quietly. What replaced the drumbeat is a fact with a picture in it — bakers starting at 3 a.m. — which is more persuasive than any adjective stack, because it's checkable and it costs the bakery something.

The adjudication principle for the owner: alliteration is seasoning measured in words, not sentences. If a reader can count the pattern, there is too much of it. The reader should taste it and never notice the cook counting.
Three sentences from a grant draft are in sentences.txt. Each one buries its most important point in the middle. Read them and show me the fix for each.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
1. The clinic, which has operated in the county for twenty years and serves 900 families, is requesting $40,000 to keep its weekend hours.
2. We trained, over the course of a long and difficult winter, forty new reading tutors.
3. After months of negotiation, the lease, which includes the garden and the workshop, was finally signed by both parties in June.

Each sentence hides its headline inside a subordinate clause or a pile of front matter. Ends are where emphasis lives, so the fix in all three is the same surgery: move the point to the end.

**1.** Buried: the request ($40,000, weekend hours) sits after a twenty-year history lesson. Fixed: "The clinic has served 900 families in this county for twenty years. It is requesting $40,000 to keep its weekend hours." Two sentences — the history now *earns* the ask instead of delaying it.

**2.** Buried: "forty new reading tutors" — the achievement — trails a weather report. Fixed: "Over one long, difficult winter, we trained forty new reading tutors." The winter becomes the frame; the number lands last, where numbers in fundraising sentences belong.

**3.** Buried: the signing itself, the actual news, is the last thing after lease contents. Fixed: "After months of negotiation, both parties signed the lease in June — the garden and the workshop included." The event leads; the detail rides behind a dash, present but demoted.

The pattern to spot in your own drafts: if the sentence's most newsworthy word appears before the final clause, the sentence is built backwards. Rebuild from the end.

My resume bullets are all over the place: 'Responsible for training new hires. Increased ticket resolution by 30%. I also handled the weekend schedule and was the person who wrote the team handbook.' A recruiter friend said 'make them parallel.' Do it and explain what that even means here.

Parallel, fixed:

"Trained new hires on the support team. Raised ticket resolution by 30 percent. Managed the weekend schedule. Wrote the team handbook."

What "parallel" means on a resume specifically: every bullet starts with the same grammatical shape — here, a past-tense action verb with the subject ("I") deleted. Your originals used four different shapes: a responsibility phrase ("Responsible for..."), a result, a chatty full sentence ("I also handled..."), and a relative clause ("was the person who..."). A recruiter scanning the column has to restart their reading four times.

Two of the rewrites did quiet extra work. "Responsible for training" became "Trained" — "responsible for" is the weakest opener in resume writing because it describes a job description, not an achievement. And "was the person who wrote the handbook" became "Wrote the team handbook" — five words doing the work of nine, and the authorship claim is actually *stronger* stated flatly.

Keep the 30 percent exactly where it is: it's the only number on the list, and in a parallel column a single number glows. That's an argument for getting numbers onto your other bullets, not for moving this one.

My blog draft is dash-happy: 'The market — which opens at dawn — is run by the Nguyen family — who have farmed the valley for decades — and their stall — the one by the gate — sells out of greens by nine.' Even I lose the thread. Fix the punctuation, keep the facts.

Fixed:

"The market opens at dawn. It's run by the Nguyen family, who have farmed the valley for decades. Their stall, the one by the gate, sells out of greens by nine."

Your original nested three interruptions inside one sentence, and the main clause ("the market... is run by...") got split so far apart that the reader had to hold the subject in memory across two detours. Em dashes are trapdoors: one pair per sentence is a limit most prose should respect, because each pair asks the reader to pause the main thought, visit a side room, and find their way back.

Notice the fix didn't delete any facts — it promoted two of the side rooms into their own sentences (the dawn opening, the family's history), where they read as information instead of interruption. The one aside that stayed in commas ("the one by the gate") is short and truly parenthetical: the sentence survives intact if you lift it out.

That's the test for any aside: lift it out. If the sentence still stands and the aside is under six words, commas are fine. If the aside deserves a breath of its own, give it a sentence.

For a writing class exercise, I need one paragraph about a community garden workday written three ways — first person, second person, third person — with a note on what each version does to the reader. The facts: on Saturday, volunteers weeded the beds, repaired a fence, and shared a tomato harvest.

The three versions:

**First person:** "I spent Saturday weeding the long beds with my neighbors. My knees ached by noon, but then we fixed the fence together, and I went home with a bag of tomatoes we'd all grown."

**Second person:** "You spend Saturday weeding the long beds. Your knees ache by noon. But then the fence is fixed, many hands making it quick, and you carry home a bag of tomatoes you helped grow."

**Third person:** "On Saturday, volunteers weeded the long beds and repaired the fence. By noon the work was done, and the tomato harvest was divided among everyone who had helped."

What each does: first person is a *testimony* — it asks to be believed, and its authority is "I was there." It's the warmest and the least verifiable. Second person is an *invitation or a simulation* — it conscripts the reader into the scene, which is why instructions and ads love it; notice it also feels slightly bossy, because it tells you what you did. Third person is a *report* — it can be checked, quoted, and filed, and it's the only version a newspaper could print; it's also the only one where no one seems to have knees.
