Same facts throughout. Person isn't a style preference — it's a choice about the reader's seat: witness, participant, or audience.
A memo from our facilities office is in memo.txt. My boss says it 'hides people.' Read it and rewrite it so we can tell who did what.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: MEMO: It has been decided that the loading dock schedule will be revised. It was determined that deliveries were being delayed. Going forward, it is expected that the new schedule will be followed, and it should be noted that concerns may be raised through the usual channels.

Rewritten with the people put back:

"MEMO: I have revised the loading dock schedule, effective Monday. Our delivery logs show trucks waited an average of 40 minutes last month because two vendors were booked into the same slot — that was my office's error. The new schedule separates them. If it causes a problem for your crew, bring it to me, Dana Whitfield, by Friday and I will adjust it."

Your boss is right, and the hiding has a grammar: the original is built entirely from agentless constructions — "it has been decided," "it was determined," "it is expected," "may be raised." Decided by whom? Expected by whom? That fog is sometimes carelessness and sometimes strategy, but it always costs the reader the same thing: there's no one to ask, thank, or push back on.

The rewrite names an actor for every verb that matters: *I* revised, *my office* erred, *you* bring problems to *Dana Whitfield*. Notice it also got more honest — the delay got a cause and an owner. Agentless prose doesn't just hide people; it hides causality, because causes usually have names. Where a memo needs accountability, name the actor. Save "we" and "it was decided" for decisions that genuinely belong to everyone.

My paragraph about our town's water tower is a hedge farm: 'It could perhaps be argued that the water tower might possibly be considered something of a local landmark, in a sense, by some residents.' I actually believe it's a landmark — the town put it on the welcome sign. Tighten it to my real confidence level.

Tightened:

"The water tower is a local landmark — the town put it on the welcome sign."

Count the hedges in your original: *could, perhaps, be argued, might, possibly, be considered, something of, in a sense, by some residents* — nine layers of retreat around a claim you have documentary evidence for. Stacked hedges don't read as care; they read as a writer who won't stand behind anything, and readers discount *all* of it, including the parts that are true.

The rewrite does two things. It states the claim at full strength, and then it does the work hedges pretend to do: it gives the *evidence*. "The town put it on the welcome sign" is worth more than any calibration word, because a reader can check it.

The rule isn't "never hedge" — it's that a hedge should mark a specific, real gap in your knowledge, and there should be at most one per claim. When you catch yourself stacking them, ask what evidence would let you drop them. Usually you already have it. You did here: it's on the sign.

Opposite problem: my draft for the neighborhood newsletter says 'The new traffic light at Elm and 4th has eliminated accidents at the intersection.' It went in two weeks ago. Even I know that's too strong. Give it the hedge it's missing without gutting it.

Calibrated version:

"In the two weeks since the traffic light went in at Elm and 4th, there have been no reported accidents at the intersection — a good early sign, though two quiet weeks can't prove the problem is solved."

Your original made three silent leaps: from *two weeks* to *forever* ("has eliminated"), from *reported* to *actual* (accidents nobody reported don't exist in your sentence), and from *correlation* to *cause* (maybe traffic was just light). The rewrite patches exactly those three seams, no more: "in the two weeks since" bounds the time; "reported" bounds the evidence; "can't prove" bounds the conclusion.

Notice the sentence didn't get weaker in the way writers fear — it got *more* informative, because now it tells the reader the sample size. An honest hedge is a measurement, not an apology. The gutting version would be "the light may possibly have helped somewhat" — all fog, no numbers. Keep the strong observation (zero accidents, named corner, named period) and hedge only the inference drawn from it. That's the whole craft: facts at full strength, conclusions at evidence strength.

Our PTA newsletter draft on the later school start time says: 'Greedy administrators want to push back start times to save bus money, leaving exhausted parents scrambling while our kids' education suffers.' I agree with the parents' side, honestly, but the newsletter goes to everyone and should describe the issue fairly. Rewrite neutrally without making it toothless.

Neutral version:

"The district has proposed moving the high school start time from 7:30 to 8:45. Administrators say the change would let bus routes run in tiers, saving an estimated $400,000 a year, and point to research linking later starts to better-rested teenagers. Many parents oppose the change: a later start means a later dismissal, which collides with jobs, sports, and younger siblings' schedules, and some question whether the bus savings will materialize. The board votes on the proposal March 18."

The loaded words and what replaced them: "greedy administrators" — a motive assigned, not a fact — became "administrators say," followed by their actual argument in its strongest form (the savings figure, the sleep research). "Leaving exhausted parents scrambling" became the parents' real, checkable concerns (dismissal time, jobs, siblings) — which are *stronger* than the adjectives were, because a reader can verify them against their own life. "Our kids' education suffers" — a conclusion dressed as a fact — was cut; neither side's evidence in your draft supports it.

Notice the neutral version isn't toothless: the parents' case gets the last substantive word, and the closing date gives everyone the action that matters. Neutrality isn't splitting the difference or draining the color. It's refusing to assign motives and letting each side's best evidence stand in the open — readers can tell when you've done it, and they trust the next issue more.

I write instructions for a community bike-repair co-op. Half my drafts sound like a manual ('The cable is inserted through the housing. The bolt is then tightened.') and half sound like a friend ('Pop the cable through the housing and snug up that bolt.'). Which voice should the co-op use, and show me the difference on one step.

For a co-op — where the reader is a neighbor standing at a workstand, possibly nervous — the friend's voice wins, and here's the same step in both so you can feel why:

**Manual:** "The cable is inserted through the housing. The barrel adjuster is turned counterclockwise until tension is achieved."

**Friend:** "Feed the cable through the housing. Now turn the barrel adjuster counterclockwise — lefty-loosey — until the cable is taut and the lever feels firm."

The manual's passive voice hides the actor, which in instructions is a real defect: "the cable is inserted" doesn't tell a beginner *who* inserts it, and beginners are exactly the readers who need to be told it's them. The friend's version uses imperative verbs aimed at *you*, and it adds the thing manuals never do — a way to check ("until the lever feels firm"). Tension isn't visible; firmness is feelable.

One caution so the friend's voice stays useful: keep the technical terms exact ("barrel adjuster," "counterclockwise") and let the warmth live in the verbs and the checks, not in nicknames for parts. Friendly and precise aren't opposites. In instructions, precise *is* friendly — it means the reader succeeds.

Our nonprofit's annual letter says: 'We are proud to announce that we have once again exceeded our goals, having served over 2,000 families this year through our network of partners.' The director wants it more personal but keeps the 'we.' I think the 'we' is part of the problem. Show her.

The "we" is doing two jobs in that sentence, and one of them is hiding. Show her this side-by-side:

**Original:** "We are proud to announce that we have once again exceeded our goals, having served over 2,000 families this year through our network of partners."

**Personal:** "I'm writing because our small team — four staff, thirty-one volunteers — helped 2,043 families this year, more than we aimed for. I want to tell you about one of them. Her name is Alina, and she found us in February with a shutoff notice and a baby."

What the institutional "we" concealed: who is speaking (a person? a board? a logo?), how big the operation is ("network of partners" sounds like hundreds; it's thirty-five people), and whether anyone in particular is proud. The rewrite doesn't abandon "we" — it *earns* it, by first establishing an "I" who can vouch for the group, and a size the reader can picture.

Two smaller upgrades came free: "over 2,000" became the exact 2,043 (round numbers in annual letters read as estimates; exact ones read as counted), and the letter now has somewhere to go — a named person — instead of ending at the organization's own pride. The rule for the director: institutional "we" is fine for policies and apologies, where the organization truly acts as one. For gratitude and storytelling, a named human has to hold the pen first.

I write the weather blurbs for our town paper's website. Yesterday I wrote 'Rain is certain tomorrow and flooding will occur in low areas.' We got rain, no flooding, and readers are teasing us. How do forecasters phrase this stuff so they're honest without sounding wishy-washy?

Forecasters survive on calibrated words — each phrase has an agreed strength. Your sentence used the two strongest settings ("certain," "will occur") for a forecast that deserved the middle ones. Recalibrated:

"Rain is likely tomorrow — an 80 percent chance through the afternoon. Low-lying areas could see standing water, and the creek may rise; major flooding is not expected."

The ladder, so you can reuse it: *certain / will* means it's effectively already decided — save it for what's upstream and observed. *Likely* means roughly 7 or 8 chances in 10. *Could / may* marks a real possibility that isn't the main expectation. And the strongest honesty move in the blurb is the closing negative — "major flooding is not expected" — which tells readers what *not* to worry about. Your original left the worst case unbounded, so readers filled it in themselves and then blamed you for their version.

Notice the calibrated version isn't wishy-washy: it's *more* specific than yours (a percentage, a time window, named places). Wishy-washy is vagueness about everything. Calibration is precision about the evidence and honesty about the odds — readers forgive a wrong forecast with honest odds. They don't forgive a certainty that fails.

I'm moderating a neighborhood forum and need to post a summary of the bike-lane fight. My draft: 'Cyclists demand the city sacrifice parking for their hobby lanes, while hardworking residents who actually pay taxes on this street are ignored again.' I typed it angry. Give me the moderator version.

Moderator version:

"The city has proposed converting the parking lane on Elm Street into a protected bike lane. Supporters — including the cycling coalition and several Elm Street residents — argue the street's two recent cyclist injuries show the current design is unsafe, and that the library lot two blocks away can absorb the parking. Opponents — including other Elm Street residents and the bakery and hardware store — argue their customers and deliveries depend on street parking, and that the library lot is full on weekends. The city planner takes comments until May 30; the council decides in June."

The repairs, since a moderator's neutrality has to be visible: "cyclists" versus "hardworking residents who actually pay taxes" framed one side as outsiders and the other as citizens — the rewrite puts *residents on both sides*, which happens to be true. "Hobby lanes" and "sacrifice" were motive words; they're replaced by each side's stated, checkable argument (injuries, the lot's capacity, deliveries, weekend fullness). Both sides get the same sentence architecture — argue + evidence — because lopsided structure is bias even when the words are clean.

And the post ends with the process (comment deadline, decision date), which is a moderator's real job: not to referee the truth of the claims, but to make sure the fight happens with both cases stated fairly and a date attached. Your angry draft wasn't wrong about your opinion. It was wrong for the chair you're sitting in.

I have to write about our town's new compost program twice: once for the sanitation department's report, once for the neighborhood association that campaigned for it. Same facts: 1,200 households enrolled in the first quarter; contamination rate 6 percent; the program costs $9 per household per month. Show me both stances on the same facts.

Same facts, two stances:

**Report stance (sanitation department):** "In its first quarter, the compost program enrolled 1,200 households. The contamination rate was 6 percent, within the range the sorting facility can process. Cost is $9 per household per month, in line with the projection adopted in the budget."

**Advocacy stance (neighborhood association):** "In just three months, 1,200 of our households — nearly a third of the neighborhood — started composting. Our contamination rate is 6 percent, cleaner than the city projected, and the whole thing costs each household $9 a month: less than two cups of coffee to keep tons of food waste out of the landfill."

Watch what changed and what didn't. The numbers are identical and equally accurate in both — stance never licenses new facts. What moved is *framing around* the facts: the report compares each figure to an operational standard (facility range, budget projection) because its reader asks "is it under control?" The advocate compares them to a story (a third of the neighborhood, two cups of coffee, the landfill) because its reader asks "did we do something that matters?"

Even the 6 percent reads differently: the report calls it "within range" (reassurance), the advocate calls it "cleaner than projected" (pride) — both true, neither neutral. There is no stance-free version of a fact in prose; there's only the discipline of keeping the facts themselves identical whichever stance you take. That's the line between framing and spin.

I supervise a warehouse. A pallet jack clipped a rack yesterday, nobody hurt, some boxes damaged. My draft report says: 'There was a near-miss incident involving equipment and the racking in aisle 4, which could have been serious, and everyone should be more careful.' My safety manager says that's not an incident report. Show me what one actually sounds like.

Your safety manager is right: your draft is an opinion about an incident, not a report of one. The genre has a strict voice — facts only, in time order, no adjectives doing verdict work:

"INCIDENT REPORT — March 3, 14:20. Location: Aisle 4, rack bay 12. Operator J. Ruiz was moving a loaded pallet jack east along aisle 4 when the right fork struck the upright of bay 12 at approximately 0.5 m height. The upright is bent inward roughly 3 cm. Six cartons on the pallet were crushed; contents (canned goods) undamaged. No injuries. The area was taped off at 14:35. Photos attached. Bay 12 is out of service pending inspection."

What the genre strips out: "near-miss" (a classification, not a fact), "could have been serious" (speculation), and "everyone should be more careful" (a recommendation wearing a report's clothes — recommendations go in a separate document where they can be assigned and dated). What it adds: times, measurements, a name, a sequence, and the state of things at the end. An incident report is written for a reader who wasn't there and may have to act on it in six months — an insurer, an inspector, a lawyer. Its voice is a camera that can count. If a sentence couldn't be verified from the photos and the clock, it doesn't belong.

I'm writing a eulogy paragraph for my neighbor, an ordinary man — a mailman for 30 years, grew tomatoes, fixed things for people on the street. Everything I draft comes out grand and fake: 'He was a pillar of the community whose generosity touched countless lives.' Help me write about the actual man.

The grand version fails because it's interchangeable — it could be read over anyone, so it's about no one. Eulogies work in the opposite direction: one true, small, checkable detail is worth more than any pillar.

"Walter carried our mail for thirty years, which means he knew this street in the order it woke up. He knew whose dog would be at the fence and whose porch light meant someone was home sick. Every August he left tomatoes on doorsteps without knocking — if you thanked him, he'd say the garden 'got ahead of him,' as if the tomatoes had done it themselves. He fixed my gate latch twice. The second time, he brought his own screws and waved off the money the same way he'd wave from the truck, like it was nothing. It wasn't nothing. It's most of what a street is."

Notice the machinery: "pillar of the community" became the route order, the porch lights, the August tomatoes — the same claim (he held this street together) made entirely of evidence. Even the closing generalization ("most of what a street is") is earned, because it arrives *after* the screws and the tomatoes and points back at them. Grand words at a funeral aren't wrong because they're large; they're wrong because they're first. Specifics first, and if a large sentence is still needed, it will write itself at the end.

I run a small landscaping company. We damaged a client's irrigation line and she found out from her water bill, not from us — that's the worst part. I need to write the apology letter. What does a real one contain?

A real apology letter has three parts, in order, and fails if any one is missing or padded. Here it is for your situation:

"Dear Mrs. Donnelly,

On May 6, our crew cut through a section of your irrigation line while edging the south bed. We did not tell you. You found out from your water bill, which means you also found out we stayed quiet — and I understand that may be the part that's hardest to forgive.

The responsibility is ours, mine specifically. The line was marked on our work plan and the crew lead did not check it; the decision not to mention a suspected nick when we saw wet soil was mine, and it was wrong.

Here is what we are doing: our plumber will replace the full section, at our cost, on a day you choose this week. We will reimburse the difference on your water bill — send us a copy, or give us the amount and we'll take your word. And I have changed our closing routine: the crew now walks the beds with the homeowner's plan before we leave any site.

I'm sorry. — Tom Ellery, Ellery Landscaping"

The three parts: acknowledgment (what happened, including the concealment — naming the worst part yourself, before she has to), responsibility (a named person and a specific failure, not "mistakes were made"), and repair (concrete, costed, scheduled, plus the systemic fix). Most failed apologies are heavy on part one and vapor on part three. The repair section is where an apology stops being a feeling and becomes a fact she can hold you to.

I'm writing a recommendation letter for a former employee applying to manage a bakery. My draft says she's 'an outstanding, exceptional, wonderful team player with amazing energy and a fantastic attitude.' Her actual record: she trained nine new hires, ran the shop alone on Sundays for a year, and caught an ordering error that saved us real money. The letter sounds like I'm lying. Why?

Because adjectives are unverifiable and hiring managers discount them to zero — a stack of superlatives reads as either exaggeration or a favor being done. Her record is *better* than your adjectives. Let it speak:

"I recommend Ana Ruiz without reservation. She worked for me for three years at Corner Crust Bakery. In that time she trained nine new hires — every one of them still works in this trade, which tells you something about how she teaches. For her last year she ran the shop alone on Sundays, our second-busiest day, including the register and the ovens. Last spring she caught a duplicate standing order that had been billing us twice for flour; fixing it saved us about $400 a month. If I had a manager's opening, I would hire her back before advertising it."

The principle: a recommendation is evidence with a signature. Each claim here can be pictured and most can be checked — nine hires, Sundays alone, $400 a month. Even the one opinion sentence ("I would hire her back") lands as evidence because it's a statement about *your* behavior, which the reader can weigh.

Keep one warm line if you like — warmth isn't the problem — but put it where warmth belongs, at the end, after the facts have made it believable. "Amazing energy" is a claim. Running a bakery alone on Sundays is energy, demonstrated.

I need one paragraph for a grant proposal to a state arts foundation. My draft, in my normal voice: 'Our little theater has been putting on plays in the old grange hall for twelve years and people around here really love it. We'd like money to fix the roof and put in better seats.' I know funders don't talk like me. Translate it into funder dialect without making things up.

Funder dialect, same facts, nothing invented:

"For twelve years, the Grange Hall Players have provided the only live theater programming in Hart County, presenting four productions annually in a 120-seat hall owned by the county grange association. Capital support is requested for two deferred-maintenance needs — roof replacement and audience seating — that directly affect the organization's ability to serve its current audience safely and to meet accessibility standards."

The translation rules: funders read for *need, population, and fit with their mission*, in that order — so your "people around here really love it" became a verifiable service claim ("the only live theater programming in Hart County"), which is the strongest sentence in the paragraph and was hiding in your draft as a feeling. "Fix the roof and put in better seats" became "deferred maintenance" and "accessibility standards" — not inflation, but the categories the funder's own guidelines score against; you're naming your facts in their vocabulary so their rubric can find them.

One caution: dialect translation must stop at vocabulary and order. The moment it starts generating facts (attendance figures you don't have, needs you haven't assessed), it becomes fiction in formal dress — and program officers can smell it. Everything above was already true in your version. It just wasn't *legible* to the reader who scores it.

Every love letter I draft sounds like a greeting card: 'You are my everything, my sun and stars, I can't imagine life without you.' My partner deserves better than a card. We've been together six years. What makes a love letter actually work?

Specificity and restraint — the two things greeting cards can't sell. A card has to fit everyone; a letter only has to fit one person, and that's its whole power. A draft built on that principle:

"Six years, and the thing I keep coming back to is the night the car died outside Prescott. You didn't panic. You made tea on that little stove in the dark like we were camping on purpose, and we ate gas-station peaches and you said, 'Well, the trip improved.' That's who you are in every hard week since: the person who decides the trip improved. I don't tell you enough that I notice it. I'm noticing it now."

Why it works where the card language doesn't: "my sun and stars" could be said to anyone, by anyone, which means it certifies nothing. The Prescott night could only be said to one person on earth — it's evidence, and love letters persuade the way recommendations do, by exhibit. Restraint does the rest: no "forever," no "everything," one remembered scene and one claim about her character drawn from it. The claim is enormous ("in every hard week since") but it's *argued*, not asserted.

The exercise, if you want your own version: pick the memory you'd save if you could only save one, write it plainly, and let one sentence say what it taught you about them. Cut every sentence that could be mailed to a stranger.
Our IT postmortem summary is in postmortem.txt. It reads like a blame document and the team is dreading publishing it internally. Read it and show me the genre fix.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: On Tuesday the payments service went down for 3 hours because an engineer deployed an untested config change during peak hours, despite warnings. The team failed to notice the alerts for 40 minutes. Service was eventually restored.

The genre fix: a postmortem's voice is blameless not as a kindness but as an engineering requirement — people hide facts from documents that punish, and hidden facts are how the outage happens twice. Same events, postmortem voice:

"On Tuesday, the payments service was unavailable for 3 hours (11:04–14:02). A config change, deployed during peak hours, set the connection limit to 10 instead of 1,000. The change had not passed through staging because the staging environment had been down for two days and the deploy process allows skipping it without an approval flag. Alerts fired at 11:06 but routed to a channel the on-call rotation no longer monitors. The service was restored by reverting the change. Actions: (1) deploys blocked when staging is down, owner: platform lead, by May 1; (2) alert routing audited weekly, owner: on-call lead."

What changed grammatically is the point: "an engineer deployed an untested change despite warnings" became a chain of *system* facts — the wrong value, the down staging environment, the process that *allowed* the skip, the unmonitored channel. Your original asks "whose fault"; the postmortem asks "what made this error easy to make and hard to catch," and every answer it finds is fixable. "The team failed to notice" becomes a routing fact with an owner and a remedy.

Note what blameless doesn't mean: soft. The postmortem version is *more* damning about the process than yours was about the person, and it ends with dated, owned actions. That's the genre: maximum accountability, zero defendants.

Second eulogy this year — this one for my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Abernathy, who died at 91. My instinct is to write about education in general and how teachers shape lives. Talk me out of it and show me the paragraph.

Talking you out of it is easy: "teachers shape lives" is true of all of them and therefore says nothing about *her* — and at 91, what the room wants is Mrs. Abernathy back for one more minute, in detail. The paragraph:

"Mrs. Abernathy kept a jar of pencil stubs on her desk, because in her room you never threw away a tool that still worked. She taught forty years of fourth graders their times tables by making us chant them while we marched around the room, and I can still hear her shoes keeping time. When my father was in the hospital that spring, she didn't make a speech about it. She just moved my desk closer to the window 'for the light,' and stayed ten minutes late every day until he came home. I was nine. I understood exactly what she was doing, and so did she, and neither of us ever mentioned it."

The method is the same as any good eulogy: general claims about teachers are replaced by her *practices* — the pencil jar (thrift as a philosophy), the marching times tables (her pedagogy in one image), and the desk moved "for the light" (kindness that protected a child's dignity by giving itself a cover story). That last detail does more than any paragraph about shaping lives: it shows *how* she shaped one.

If you want one general sentence, put it where generals belong — last, and pointed back at the evidence: "That is what a teacher is, when the word means everything it can." After the pencil jar, the room will believe it.

I'm writing a scholarship recommendation for a student. The form asks for 'a specific instance that demonstrates character.' All I have in my draft is 'She is honest, hardworking, and a joy to teach.' The committee has read that sentence ten thousand times. What do I write instead?

You write the instance — committees ask for one because it's the only part of the form that can't be faked cheaply. If your student is who you say she is, there's a moment; find it and narrate it plainly:

"Last October, grading a midterm, I marked one of Maya's answers correct that she knew was wrong — a misread rubric on my part, worth six points. She came to my office after class, showed me the rubric, and asked me to take the points off, because two classmates had lost points on the same question graded the other way. I have taught for nineteen years. Students have appealed grades in my office many times, in one direction only. Maya is the only one who has ever appealed her own grade *down*, on behalf of other people."

Why this outperforms "honest, hardworking, a joy to teach": the adjectives claim a trait; the story *stages* it, with stakes (six points, her own GPA) and a witness (you, with nineteen years of comparison class — your experience becomes the measuring instrument, which is what a recommender is for). "On behalf of other people" is the sentence the committee will quote to each other, and you could never have reached it by adjective.

Practical method for finding the instance: ask yourself when the student surprised you. Character shows at the moment behavior costs something. If no moment exists, the honest letter says less — but it almost always exists; it's filed under memories, not under traits.

My bakery sold a batch of sourdough last Saturday that was badly underproofed — gummy inside. People paid $9 a loaf. I want to post a public apology on our shop page. Draft it the way you'd want to read it as a customer.

As a customer, this is what would bring me back:

"About Saturday's sourdough: it wasn't right. We rushed the proof on a cold morning and the loaves came out gummy inside. That's on us — the bread told us it needed more time and we didn't listen. If you bought one, bring back the loaf, the wrapper, or just tell us at the counter, and we'll replace it or refund you, your choice, no receipt needed. We've changed the Saturday bake: the dough now proofs overnight, whatever the morning looks like. Sorry we sold you bread we wouldn't serve at home. — The Corner Crust team"

The parts, from the customer's side of the counter: the defect named in plain words ("gummy inside") — no "quality issue," no "inconsistency," because customers know what gummy means and euphemism tells them you're managing them. The cause admitted at the level of the real failure (we rushed; we overrode what we knew). The remedy made effortless — no receipt, their choice of replacement or refund, even the wrapper suffices — because every condition you put on a remedy reads as a hope that they won't claim it. And the systemic fix, stated in one line, so the apology ends pointing forward.

The standard it ends on ("bread we wouldn't serve at home") is the one line of warmth the post needs. Everything else is facts and terms. That's the ratio public apologies want.

For my fiction class, I need a short exchange at a bus stop between a teenager and his grandmother where you can tell who's speaking with no dialogue tags at all. Then explain the levers, because my instructor will ask.

The exchange:

"Bus is late."
"The bus is not late, Marcus. We are early, because someone set the alarm for six and then argued with it for twenty minutes."
"Okay, but if it doesn't come by seven-thirty, I'm gonna be late for first period and Mr. Doyle's gonna write me up."
"Mr. Doyle will survive the shock. Stand up straight — you're slouching into the next generation."
"Grandma."
"I'm just saying, a boy who can sleep through three alarms can survive one tardy slip."

The levers, for your instructor: **vocabulary** — hers is precise and slightly formal ("argued with it," "survive the shock"), his is compressed and current ("gonna," "write me up"). **Sentence shape** — she speaks in complete, balanced sentences with subordinate clauses; he speaks in fragments and run-ons that trail into consequences. **What each one talks about** — he reports his immediate problem; she reframes it from altitude, which is what grandmothers in fiction are *for*. **The comeback structure** — his one-word "Grandma." only works because the reader already knows who's exasperated, which is the proof the voices are distinct: the tags became unnecessary two lines in.

The test for tagless dialogue: cover the names and read aloud. If you ever have to stop and work out who spoke, the diction isn't doing its job yet.

My novel has a character from rural Mississippi. A beta reader said my dialect writing is 'a minstrel show in print.' My line was: 'Ah reckon y'all gonna be fixin' tuh leave fo' de sun go down, ain't ya?' Show me what she means and how to do it with restraint.

Your beta reader is pointing at *eye dialect* — respelling words to mimic pronunciation. It's a minstrel-show inheritance because its real function was historically to mark a speaker as uneducated for a reader presumed standard. Watch the same line in three passes:

**Heavy (yours):** "Ah reckon y'all gonna be fixin' tuh leave fo' de sun go down, ain't ya?" — nearly every word respelled. The reader decodes instead of hearing, and the character's intelligence gets taxed for the effort.

**Restrained:** "I reckon y'all will want to be leaving before the sun goes down." — two markers only: "reckon" (a word choice, not a respelling) and "y'all." Everything else is standard spelling carrying regional *grammar and rhythm*.

**By syntax alone:** "Before the sun goes down'd be the time to leave, I'd reckon." — the fronted time phrase and the trailing tag do the regional work; spelling is untouched.

Why restraint works better: real dialect lives mostly in word choice, idiom, and sentence rhythm — things that survive standard spelling — while pronunciation is the shallowest layer and the one readers stumble over. Two or three consistent markers and the reader's ear supplies the accent themselves, in their own head, at full dignity. The character should sound like a *place*. Your heavy version makes him sound like a *spelling lesson* — and readers blame the character, not the author, which is exactly the unfairness your beta reader flagged.

I was interviewed for a local history podcast about restoring our theater. My answer to 'why did it take ten years?' came out as: 'Well, so, the thing is, we started in 2014, and there was the roof, and then funding fell through in 2016, which was hard, and we had volunteers, lots of them, and the historical society got involved, and there were permits, so many permits, and eventually in 2024 we reopened, which was great.' The host wants a tight version for the transcript. Cut it without changing what I said.

Tightened:

"We started in 2014. The roof came first; then funding fell through in 2016, which nearly ended it. What carried the project through was volunteers — and, eventually, the historical society. The permits took years on their own. We reopened in 2024."

What got cut is connective tissue, not content: the "well, so, the thing is" preamble (spoken throat-clearing — it buys the speaker time and costs the reader attention), the repeated "and then / and" chains (speech strings events with *and*; prose sorts them with punctuation), and "which was hard / which was great" — evaluations the facts already deliver. What I did *not* cut: any fact, any date, the near-failure in 2016, or the credit to the volunteers. And one phrase got slightly *strengthened*, honestly: "which nearly ended it" — your original said the funding loss "was hard"; in context (you then describe years of struggle) "nearly ended it" is what you meant, but flag it: if it didn't nearly end the project, keep "which set us back years." Tightening may compress a speaker's words; it may never upgrade their claims.

The test after any edit of spoken words: could the speaker read the tight version and say "yes, that's what I said" — not "that's what I should have said"? The first is editing. The second is ghostwriting, and transcripts don't allow it.

I'm writing a profile of our mayor for the town paper and I need to shorten her quote. What she said: 'I think the budget, which as you know I've worked on for the better part of two years, is something that, when you look at the whole picture — the roads, the schools, all of it — really does reflect what this town told me it wanted when I knocked on doors in 2022.' I want to print: 'The budget reflects what this town told me it wanted.' Fair?

Fair — and it's worth seeing *why*, because the rules of quote-trimming are what stand between editing and putting words in mouths.

Your trimmed version keeps her verb, her subject, and her claim intact: budget, reflects, what the town told me it wanted. Everything you cut was scaffolding — her throat-clearing ("I think," "as you know"), her credentials aside (two years of work), and her list (roads, schools). None of it changed the direction of the sentence.

Now the lines you may not cross, with the traps in her sentence: you may not cut a *qualifier* — if she had said "the budget *mostly* reflects," the "mostly" is load-bearing and deleting it makes her more certain than she was. You may not cut a negation or a condition ("if the state money comes through"), ever. You may not stitch — joining "the budget" from the start to a phrase from a different answer, even with ellipses, manufactures a sentence she never spoke. And with ellipses, the test is whether a reader hearing the full tape would feel the printed version dealt honestly.

One more thing your version does right: you cut "when I knocked on doors in 2022" — flavor — but if the *profile's point* were her door-knocking, that phrase would be substance and cutting it would distort. Fair trimming is relative to meaning, not just grammar. When in doubt, the rule is simple: trim for length, never for advantage.
Writing exercise: a two-person scene, a pilot and a nervous passenger before takeoff, no tags, voices as different as possible. Then a line or two on how the contrast is built.

The scene:

"Wind's from the west at twelve. We'll be up in four minutes."
"Four minutes? Is that — do you always take off that fast? Not that fast is bad. Fast is probably good. Experienced, even."
"Fast is normal. Seat belt snug?"
"Snug. Very snug. I read that most incidents happen at takeoff and landing, which is — I'm not helping myself, am I?"
"You're doing fine. Watch the wing if you like. It flexes. It's built to."
"It *flexes*?"
"Like a bird's. We'll level at ten thousand and I'll turn the sign off. Then coffee."

How the contrast is built: the pilot speaks in *checklists and numbers* — short declaratives, every sentence either a fact or an instruction, nothing speculative. The passenger speaks in *spirals* — questions that answer themselves, self-corrections mid-sentence ("Not that fast is bad"), and statistics deployed as anxiety. The pilot's calm isn't described; it's enacted by sentence length — his longest line is shorter than her shortest spiral. And his one moment of warmth is technical ("It's built to") because that's the only register he has: reassurance delivered as engineering. Two voices are distinct when each character would say the *same fact* differently — "the wing flexes" is her terror and his comfort, in the same three words.
I have a shopkeeper character in a story set in coastal Maine. I don't want phonetic spelling. Give me three lines for her that suggest the place through word choice and rhythm alone.

Three lines:

"Ayuh, we've got the chowder on. Sit anywhere the light's good."
"Your boy's grown a foot since August. They do that, right about when the boots stop fitting."
"Storm's coming by Thursday, they say. Get your bread today — tomorrow the road's anybody's guess."

The suggestion works through three light touches: one signature word ("ayuh" — used once, then retired; a marker repeated every line becomes a costume), local knowledge as content (chowder, the storm, the road — she talks about what a coastal shopkeeper actually watches), and a rhythm of short, complete sentences with the occasional trailing observation ("They do that") that has the cadence of someone who's said these things ten thousand times. Nothing is respelled — "grown," "coming," "tomorrow" all keep their standard forms, because the reader's ear will do the accent work for free once the vocabulary and rhythm point it there.

The discipline: choose two or three markers and hold them *consistently* rather than layering on new ones. Consistency reads as a person; accumulation reads as a performance.

A transcript of my podcast answer is in answer.txt — it's about why I left teaching to open a bakery. The show notes need a tightened version. Read it and cut it to its core without changing my meaning.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: So I taught middle school for, like, eleven years, and I loved the kids, I really did, but the grading — stacks and stacks of it, every night, every weekend — and I started baking on Sundays just to do something with my hands that was finished when it was finished, you know? And people started asking for loaves, and then a cafe asked, and then one morning I just knew. So I saved for two years and I opened the bakery in 2019.

Tightened:

"I taught middle school for eleven years. I loved the kids. But the grading never ended — every night, every weekend. I started baking on Sundays just to do something with my hands that was finished when it was finished. Then people started asking for loaves. Then a cafe asked. I saved for two years and opened the bakery in 2019."

Every fact survived: eleven years, the kids, the grading, the Sundays, the requests, the cafe, the two years of saving, 2019. What left: the spoken filler ("like," "you know," "I really did," "I just knew") and the breathless single-sentence run, which in print reads as rambling even though it sounded fine aloud — speech gets rhythm from the voice; print has to build it from punctuation, so I gave her sentences full stops where her voice took breaths.

One phrase I protected absolutely: "finished when it was finished." That's the quotable core — the whole career change in six words — and it's the line a careless edit might have smoothed into "something tangible." When you tighten spoken words, the vivid, slightly unpolished phrase is usually the point. Cut around it, never through it.

Our historical society newsletter wants to quote a 1962 letter from the town founder's granddaughter. The sentence is long: 'The mill, which my grandfather built with his own hands and which employed half the town in its good years, was, though I grieve to write it, already a ruin when I last saw it in the spring of 1961, its wheel still, its windows gone to the weather.' We only have room for about half. What may we cut and what may we never cut?

A fair half-length version:

"The mill... was, though I grieve to write it, already a ruin when I last saw it in the spring of 1961, its wheel still, its windows gone to the weather."

What was cut: the whole relative clause about her grandfather building it and employing half the town — real information, but it's the part your readers mostly know, and the sentence's heart is the ruin, not the history. The ellipsis marks the cut honestly, and the surviving words are all hers, in her order.

What may never be cut, and why each is load-bearing: "though I grieve to write it" — her feeling about the fact; cutting it would make her sound detached, a change of *meaning*, not length. "Already" — one small word carrying her whole judgment that the ruin came too soon. "In the spring of 1961" — the date anchors the testimony; a quote trimmed of its when becomes unfalsifiable. And the closing pair "its wheel still, its windows gone to the weather" — cut that and you've kept her conclusion and deleted her evidence.

With historical letters there's an extra duty: the writer can't correct you. The dead get the strictest version of the rule — trim for space, never for smoothness, and if a cut changes her tone, her certainty, or her facts, the quote runs long or doesn't run.

Scene-writing problem: my two characters — a hotel manager trained in formal hospitality and a new intern — keep sounding the same in dialogue. Give me a short exchange about a lost reservation where they can't be confused, and diagnose my problem.

The exchange:

"Good evening. You have a reservation under Whitaker? Allow me a moment — I will find it, and if our system has misplaced it, we will make it right tonight."
"Oh no. Oh no no. The computer ate it? It's been doing that, it ate the Hendersons on Tuesday too —"
"Then the system and I will have a conversation later. For now: a room on the third floor, quiet end, and breakfast on the house while we sort the paperwork."
"You can just — do that? Just give them breakfast?"
"I can make a guest comfortable while a problem is being solved. That is, in fact, the entire job."

Your diagnosis: your characters sound the same because you're writing what they *say about the problem* instead of *who is speaking*. The manager's voice is built from complete sentences, future-oriented reassurance ("we will make it right"), and the professional's key move — separating the guest's comfort from the system's failure, in that order. The intern speaks in fragments, spirals, and process-leak (telling the guest the computer "ate the Hendersons too" — exactly what training exists to prevent). The comedy and the characterization are the same thing: two different relationships to the crisis.

The repair habit: for each character, fix three things before writing a scene — their sentence length, what they do under stress (procedure vs. panic), and what they'd never say. Voice is mostly the third one. The manager would never narrate the system's faults to a guest; the intern can't help it. Give your characters prohibitions and they'll separate themselves.

My writing group did an exercise where all the dialogue tags were stripped from a scene. Mine fell apart — nobody could tell my two sisters apart. What specific levers should I have built in? Use a tiny example of two sisters arguing about selling their mother's house.

The levers, with the sisters built on them:

"We should list it in spring. Spring gets the best price, and the garden will be up."
"You and your spring. You said spring about the roof, and the car, and Dad's boat."
"And I was right about the boat."
"You were right about the boat. One boat, Ruth. Everything can't wait for a season."
"Some things can. A house their mother died in can wait until the garden's up."

The levers, named so you can reuse them: **agenda** — one sister argues timing and value (price, seasons, the garden as an asset), the other argues from grievance and history (the roof, the car, the boat). Even with identical grammar, *what each one reaches for* separates them. **Signature syntax** — Ruth builds balanced, complete sentences; her sister fires short volleys and repeats phrases back with a twist ("You were right about the boat. One boat, Ruth.") — echoing-as-attack is her fingerprint. **Forms of address** — the younger uses "Ruth" as a weapon mid-argument; Ruth never names her back, which is its own characterization: the elder sister doesn't need to. **The tell in the last line** — Ruth drops into third person about "their mother" — a sudden formality that lands the emotional blow precisely because her voice has been practical until then.

Build sheet for any pair: give each a distinct sentence shape, a distinct thing they always argue *from*, and one verbal habit the other never uses. Tags become decoration instead of load-bearing walls.

Teach me the three-pass edit on my paragraph about our community garden: 'The garden was started in 2019 by a group of neighbors who wanted to grow food. It has 40 plots and a waiting list. People grow tomatoes and other vegetables there. The garden also has a shed where tools are kept and a picnic table. It has been good for the neighborhood in many ways.' Show me each pass, not just the result.

Each pass has one job, and the discipline is refusing to do the next pass's job early.

**Pass 1 — structure.** The paragraph is a list, not an arc: founding, size, crops, shed, verdict. The verdict ("good for the neighborhood") is asserted, unsupported, and last. Structure fix: move the human claim forward and let the facts serve it, and cut the shed-and-table inventory — it belongs in a facilities doc, not here. Skeleton: *what the garden is for → proof of demand → what happens there.*

**Pass 2 — sentences.** On the new skeleton, the sentences are all the same shape (subject-verb-fact). Vary them and merge the twins: "Founded in 2019 by neighbors who wanted to grow their own food, the garden now has 40 plots — and a waiting list. On summer evenings the beds are full of tomatoes, peppers, and people trading both."

**Pass 3 — words.** Only now the small change: "other vegetables" → "peppers" (a specific beats a category); "in many ways" deleted (it was the unsupported verdict sneaking back); "trading both" kept — one small charm, allowed because the facts are now solid.

Final: "Founded in 2019 by neighbors who wanted to grow their own food, the garden now has 40 plots — and a waiting list. On summer evenings the beds are full of tomatoes, peppers, and people trading both."

Why the order matters: if you'd done word-level fixes first, you'd have polished "the shed where tools are kept" beautifully — and then cut it in the structure pass. Big to small, always: structure decides what exists, sentences decide how it moves, words decide how it shines.

I'm editing my essay about my father's hardware store. There's a sentence I love: 'The store smelled of turpentine and cut pine, and the light came through the front windows in long amber bars, the way it must have in 1962.' My editor says cut it. I don't want to. Make her case — honestly — and tell me if she wins.

Her case, honestly made: your essay's argument (from everything around that sentence) is about what the store *did* — the credit it extended, the advice it gave, the town it held together. The beloved sentence is a painting hung in the middle of an argument. It stops the essay to admire the light. Worse, "the way it must have in 1962" reaches for a nostalgia the essay hasn't earned yet — it's borrowing feeling from the reader instead of building it. Sentences we love most are often the ones written for ourselves, and other readers can feel the author admiring his own work.

Does she win? Mostly. But there's a negotiation she should accept: the sentence doesn't have to die — it has to *move*. As the essay's closing image, after the argument is complete, that amber light becomes a benediction instead of an interruption, and "1962" lands as a summary of everything the essay proved about continuity. Placement is often the real edit; "cut" is just the editor's shorthand for "not here."

The test to run on any beloved sentence: cover it and read the piece. If nothing is missing, it was decoration — move it to where decoration belongs (the end) or let it go. If the piece limps without it, it was load-bearing and the editor is wrong. Yours, I suspect, is decoration — *good* decoration, which is why it hurts. The pain isn't evidence she's wrong. It's evidence you wrote one fine sentence too many for this essay's shape.

My draft announcement for our library's new evening hours is in hours.txt. Before I revise it, I want to read it the way our patrons will. Read it and annotate it with the questions a reader will actually have.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: The library is pleased to announce expanded evening hours. Starting soon, the main branch will remain open later on weeknights to better serve our community. We look forward to welcoming you during these new hours.

Reading it as a patron, here are my three questions, in the order I'd ask them — and your draft answers none of them:

**1. "Later until when?"** — the only number a patron needs, and "remain open later" withholds it. Later could be 7 or 10. This is the question the announcement exists to answer, and it's the first one a reader asks.

**2. "Starting when, exactly?"** — "starting soon" forces me to either guess or check back. A reader who has to check back usually doesn't; they just show up at the old time once, find it wrong either way, and stop trusting announcements.

**3. "Which nights — all weeknights?"** — "weeknights" hides whether Friday counts. Parents planning around a work schedule need the specific days.

Notice the shape of the problem: your draft is written in the library's voice about the library's feelings ("pleased to announce," "look forward to welcoming"), so it spends its words on the sender. The reader's questions are all requests for *numbers and days*. The revision writes itself once you've heard them: "Starting Monday, April 6, the main branch stays open until 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday." Annotating a draft with the reader's questions is the fastest revision tool there is — the questions *are* the edit list.

I have a brief for a client: 'Audience: small-business owners. Purpose: get them to book a free consultation. Register: expert but approachable, no hype.' My draft paragraph: 'Our revolutionary, game-changing platform leverages synergies to supercharge your growth journey! Book now — spots are vanishing fast!!!' Run the final-voice check on it against the brief.

Final-voice check, brief item by item:

**Audience — small-business owners: FAIL.** The draft speaks in startup-founder dialect ("growth journey," "supercharge"). Owners of actual small businesses — plumbers, bakers, dentists — don't describe their work this way and distrust copy that does.

**Purpose — book a free consultation: PARTIAL.** "Book now" is present, but the word *free* — the single most persuasive fact in the brief — never appears, and neither does *consultation*. The call to action asks for a click without naming the offer.

**Register — expert but approachable, no hype: FAIL, twice.** "Revolutionary, game-changing" is hype in its purest form, and it's also the opposite of expertise: experts specify, hype adjectives. "Spots are vanishing fast!!!" adds manufactured urgency — with three exclamation points — that an approachable expert would never use and this audience can smell.

Verdict: the draft matches the brief on zero of three counts, which is common — drafts drift toward the writer's excitement, briefs describe the reader's needs. A passing version: "We help small businesses sort out their bookkeeping before tax season gets expensive. The first consultation is free, takes thirty minutes, and you'll leave with a written list of what we'd fix first — whether you hire us or not." Expert (specific, bounded claims), approachable (plain words), and the free offer up front. The check takes two minutes and should be the last thing any draft goes through: hold each line of the brief against the text and demand evidence.

Do the three-pass edit on my product description for handmade soap: 'Our soap is made by hand in small batches using natural ingredients. It comes in many scents like lavender and others. It is gentle on skin and good for gifts. Buy some today for yourself or someone you love.' It sells okay but it sounds like every other soap.

**Pass 1 — structure.** The paragraph is a circle of general claims (handmade, natural, gentle, giftable) with no anchor fact and no order. Structure fix: lead with the most specific true thing, then qualities, then use. What's specific here? "Small batches" is the seed of it — if it's real, the batch size and the maker's hands are the story.

**Pass 2 — sentences.** Rebuilt on that order: "We make this soap in batches of forty bars, by hand, in our Vermont workshop. Each batch cures for five weeks before it's cut. Lavender is the one people reorder; the unscented bar is the one dermatologists' patients ask us for." Sentences now vary, and two of them contain *behavior* (reordering, asking) instead of claims.

**Pass 3 — words.** "Natural ingredients" — cut (unverifiable, and every soap on earth says it). "Good for gifts" — cut (the reader decides that). "Buy some today for yourself or someone you love" — replaced by nothing; the description ends on the product, and the buy button does the asking.

Final: "We make this soap in batches of forty bars, by hand, in our Vermont workshop. Each batch cures for five weeks before it's cut. Lavender is the one people reorder. The unscented bar is the one people with sensitive skin ask for by name."

Why it no longer sounds like every other soap: every generic phrase was a place where a fact could have been. Three passes, and the deepest change was pass one — deciding the description was *about* smallness and patience, not about soap in general.

My annual report for our food bank opens with a two-page anecdote about one volunteer's morning. It's a good story. My board chair says open with the numbers. I say the story is the numbers' best friend. Who's right?

You're both half right, and the resolution is a matter of *length and placement*, not principle. Your chair is right about this: two pages is not an opening, it's a hostage situation. Board members, donors, and journalists read annual reports in a specific order — they hunt for the headline figures first (households served, cost per meal, growth), and a two-page story before any number reads as concealment, as if the figures needed a warm-up act. Some will simply skip to find them, and then your story gets read resentfully or not at all.

You're right about the deeper thing: a report that is only numbers gets filed and forgotten, and the story is what a donor repeats at dinner. The synthesis used by good reports: open with one paragraph — the headline numbers, plainly — then *one page or less* of the story, told tight, then the full data. The numbers buy the story its welcome; the story gives the numbers a memory.

One more consideration for your chair: if the volunteer's morning contains a number in it ("by 7 a.m. she'd packed 200 weekend bags"), the story and the data stop being rivals. The best version of your opening anecdote is probably 600 words with three figures embedded in it. Cut it to that and the argument dissolves — she gets her numbers up front, you keep your story, and each makes the other stronger.

Here's my rental listing draft: 'Charming 2BR! Great location! Lots of light! Close to everything! Won't last!' Annotate it as a renter reading it — what will they actually want to know that I'm not telling them?

Reading as a renter, my questions arrive fast:

**"How much?"** — the listing's first fact in any renter's mind, and it's absent. No rent, no deposit, no utilities. A listing without a price isn't a listing; it's a teaser, and renters have learned teasers hide a number you'd flinch at.

**"Where, exactly?"** — "great location" and "close to everything" are the two emptiest phrases in the genre. Close to *what* — the train, a school, a highway? A neighborhood name and one true landmark would answer it. "Lots of light" has the same problem: which direction do the windows face, and is that light at 8 a.m. or 4 p.m.?

**"What's the catch?"** — "won't last!" creates pressure while providing nothing to evaluate, and five exclamation points in five lines teaches me to discount everything else in the ad. The questions you didn't answer (laundry? parking? pets? lease length? floor?) become, in a renter's mind, a list of probable no's.

The annotated revision writes itself: "2BR, second floor, $1,450/month. Maple Street, six minutes' walk to the train. South-facing living room — bright from morning. In-unit laundry, one parking spot, cats OK. Twelve-month lease, available June 1." Same apartment, probably. One version is advertising; the other is information, and renters sign leases for the second kind.

My scholarship essay brief (from my counselor): 'Audience: the foundation's readers, who read 400 essays. Purpose: show fit with their service mission. Register: personal, specific, no grand claims.' My opening: 'Since the dawn of time, humanity has yearned to serve others, and I am no exception. Service is the rent we pay for our time on earth, and my journey of service has transformed me in countless ways.' Run the check.

The check, against your counselor's three lines:

**Audience — readers of 400 essays: FAIL.** "Since the dawn of time" is, statistically, how a large share of those 400 essays begin — the cosmic opening. A reader on essay 212 has developed an immune response to it; your first sentence tells them they've read this essay before, and they'll skim the rest looking for a reason to stop.

**Purpose — show fit with a service mission: FAIL so far.** The opening names no service, no place, no person, and nothing the foundation funds. Fit can't be shown in the abstract; it requires your actual work to appear and rhyme with their actual mission.

**Register — personal, specific, no grand claims: FAIL, three for three.** "Humanity has yearned" is as grand as claims get; there's nothing personal (no "I" doing anything concrete) and nothing specific (no noun you could photograph). Even the one borrowed line — "service is the rent we pay" — is a famous quotation doing your feeling for you.

A passing opening would start where the brief points: "On Tuesdays I read with Mr. Okafor at the branch library. He's 84, he's teaching himself to use email so he can write to his grandson, and last month he sent the first one himself." Personal (a named person), specific (Tuesdays, email, last month), zero grand claims — and the fit with a service mission is *shown* in four lines instead of announced. The check's lesson generalizes: a brief is a contract, and the opening paragraph is where breaches show first.
My retirement speech for a colleague is in speech.txt — it's 200 words of thanks. Walk it through all three editing passes in front of me. I want to learn the method on my own text.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: When Frank joined the department in 1998, things were different. He has done many jobs over the years and helped many people. He was always there when you needed him. We will miss him a lot. Frank taught us many things. We wish him well in his retirement and hope he enjoys his garden and his grandchildren.

Your speech, pass by pass. The draft's problem in one line: it's all true and none of it is *Frank* — every sentence could be read at any retirement in America.

**Pass 1 — structure.** Currently: arrival, general praise, we'll miss him, lessons, good wishes. The structure has no *scene* — nothing the audience can see. Restructure around one true episode that contains the praise: Frank's first week, or the day he stayed late for someone. Structure decision: open with the episode, let the general claims follow it as conclusions, end with the garden and grandchildren (they're specific — they stay, and they move to the end where closings belong).

**Pass 2 — sentences.** The draft is six sentences of identical length and shape. On the new structure, they vary: a long storytelling sentence for the episode, then short ones for the verdicts — "He stayed. That's who he is." Short sentences after a story read as the room nodding.

**Pass 3 — words.** "Helped many people" → name one. "Taught us many things" → name the thing ("taught half this room how to read a soil report"). "Always there when you needed him" → keep — it's the one general sentence the episode will have earned.

The catch, honestly stated: passes 2 and 3 I can demonstrate, but pass 1 needs a fact I don't have — the episode. That's not a failure of the method; it's the method *finding* the real work. Three-pass editing can't invent the scene. It can only tell you the speech is missing one, which is the most useful thing an edit can say. Bring me one true Frank story and the speech finishes itself.

Final exam for myself: here's a paragraph I wrote for our historical society's newsletter, and the brief I wrote it to: 'Audience: members, mostly retired, who know the town well. Purpose: recruit two volunteers to index the photo archive. Register: warm, brief, no guilt trips.' My paragraph: 'As our beloved archive continues to grow, we must all ask ourselves whether we are doing enough. The photo collection — thousands of images of our town's rich history — sits unindexed, and without your help, these precious memories may be lost forever. Surely each of us can find a few hours for the town that gave us so much.' Grade it against the brief, line by line.

Grading against your own brief, line by line:

**"As our beloved archive continues to grow"** — *warm* ✓, but "beloved" is claimed rather than shown, and the sentence spends its length on the archive, not the reader. Brief-compliant enough to pass, barely.

**"We must all ask ourselves whether we are doing enough"** — brief violation, flagged by the brief's own words: this is a guilt trip. "No guilt trips" was your rule, and this sentence is nothing else. It also recruits nobody in particular — "we all" means no one.

**"Thousands of images... sits unindexed"** — the strongest line in the paragraph: a real fact, a real task. Purpose ✓. But "may be lost forever" inflates it — unindexed isn't lost, and your audience *knows the town well*, which per the brief means they know the photos are in acid-free boxes in a dry room. Overclaiming to experts insults them quietly.

**"Surely each of us can find a few hours for the town that gave us so much"** — second guilt trip, plus it never says the actual ask: *two* volunteers, *indexing*, a defined job. The brief's purpose was recruitment; the paragraph never makes the specific request that recruitment requires.

**Overall grade: the draft fails its own brief on the two lines the brief was most explicit about** — no guilt (violated twice) and purpose (the ask never lands). Passing version: "Our photo archive has grown to several thousand images, and most aren't indexed yet — if you know this town's faces, you're exactly who can name them. We need two volunteers, a few hours a month, coffee provided, in the back room on Tuesdays. See Marge to sign up." Warm, brief, zero guilt — and it treats the readers' knowledge as the qualification, which for this audience is the truest compliment available. You set a good brief. The draft just didn't obey it — which is why the check exists.

Our dental office's outgoing voicemail script says: 'You have reached the offices of Brightpath Dental Associates. Our hours of operation are Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. If this is a dental emergency, please hang up and dial 911. Otherwise, leave a message after the tone and a member of our team will return your call at our earliest convenience.' It sounds like a courthouse. Warm it up — but it's still a phone script people hear when they're in pain.

Warmer, same information, same safety order:

"Thanks for calling Brightpath Dental. We're open Monday to Friday, 8 to 5. If you're having a dental emergency — severe pain, swelling, a knocked-out tooth — please hang up and call 911. Otherwise, leave us a message and we'll call you back the same business day."

What changed: "You have reached the offices of" (six words of ceremony) became "Thanks for calling." "A member of our team will return your call at our earliest convenience" — the coldest phrase in business English, because "our convenience" is frankly the office's — became a commitment: "the same business day." Warmth in service scripts is mostly *specific promises* replacing vague courtesies.

What deliberately did not change: the emergency instruction stays early, stays an instruction, and even gained examples (severe pain, swelling, a knocked-out tooth) because a person in pain at 2 a.m. shouldn't have to decide whether their problem "counts" as an emergency. That's the boundary of warming a functional script: the friendliness lives in the framing; the safety content gets *clearer*, never softer.

For our library's civics corner, I need a kid-facing version (about age 10) of this: 'A bill becomes law through introduction, committee review, floor debate, passage by both chambers, and executive signature; alternatively, a two-thirds majority may override an executive veto.' Keep it accurate. Kids can tell when you're faking.

Kid-facing, and accurate:

"A law starts as an idea written down, called a bill. First, a small group of lawmakers studies it closely and asks hard questions — that's the committee. Then all the lawmakers in the first chamber talk it over and vote. If it passes, it goes to the second chamber, and they do the whole thing again. If both chambers say yes, the bill goes to the governor (or the President, for the whole country), who can sign it into law — or veto it, which means saying no. But the story doesn't have to end there: if two out of every three lawmakers in both chambers vote yes again, the bill becomes law anyway. The veto is a strong no, but it isn't the final word."

What's preserved, because kids can indeed tell: the *order* of the steps, the committee's real function (close study, hard questions — not a rubber stamp), the both-chambers requirement, and the override fraction stated as "two out of every three," which is two-thirds with the arithmetic shown. What changed is only the clothing: "executive signature" became a person signing; "passage" became voting yes.

The one simplification I'll confess: conference committees and amendments between chambers are omitted. That's a *completeness* cut, not an accuracy one — everything stated is true; not everything true is stated. That's the honest line for writing down to any audience: you may leave steps out, but you may not put false ones in.

Our ferry company had an engine failure Tuesday and cancelled six sailings. The ops report is thorough and long. The CEO needs four sentences before a press call. Facts: the 7:10 from Harland Point lost power mid-crossing, was towed in safely, no injuries; a cracked fuel line is the suspected cause; the sister ship covered three of six cancelled sailings; full refunds issued; inspection of the whole fleet ordered. Write the executive version.

Four sentences, verdict first:

"Tuesday's 7:10 sailing from Harland Point lost power mid-crossing and was towed in; all passengers are safe. We believe a cracked fuel line is the cause, and I have ordered an inspection of every vessel in the fleet before the affected ship returns to service. Our sister ship covered three of the six cancelled sailings, and every affected passenger has been refunded in full. We will publish the inspection findings when we have them."

What the executive version does that the ops report can't: it sequences by *what a listener fears*, not by chronology — safety, cause, remedy, restitution, in that order, because that's the order a press call (and a frightened public) processes them. The CEO speaks in first person for the decision ("I have ordered") because accountability at a press call must have a face; the company's "we" handles the rest.

What got cut from your facts, deliberately: the tow's duration, the crew names, the maintenance history — all legitimate ops content, none of it decision-relevant in four sentences. And note the one hedge, placed exactly: "we believe" attaches to the *suspected* cause only. Everything else stands unhedged, because everything else is known. A press statement's credibility is its hedge placement: one "believe" in the right spot makes the four certainties believable.

I write appeals for a food bank. Our standard letter leads with our mission and how wonderful giving feels. Donations are flat. A board member says our readers are skeptics now — they want to know we won't waste it. Restructure the opening for a skeptical reader.

For a skeptic, the opening has to answer the audit question before the emotion question — not because emotion doesn't matter, but because a skeptic can't feel anything until the waste question is settled:

"Last year, of every dollar given to the Harborview Food Bank, 91 cents went directly to food and distribution. We can buy in bulk at roughly a third of grocery prices, so a $50 gift puts about $150 worth of food on our shelves. We served 4,100 households in this county last year; our audited statements are on our website, and our warehouse on Dock Street is open to any donor who wants to see the operation. The other 9 cents keeps the trucks running and the lights on."

Then — and only then — the mission and the feeling, which now land on verified ground.

The structural principle: your current letter asks for trust and then offers feelings as the reward. The skeptical reader runs the sequence in reverse: evidence first, and trust as the *conclusion*. Notice the opening also concedes the overhead openly ("the other 9 cents...") instead of hiding it in a footnote — skeptics are disarmed less by a low number than by a number volunteered. And the invitation to visit the warehouse costs you nothing and outperforms any adjective: organizations that waste money do not invite donors to watch the trucks load.

A customer emailed complaining our garden center sold her a rose bush that died. My reply draft is defensive: 'Our roses are quality plants and many customers have success with them. The bush was healthy when sold. Planting conditions vary and we cannot be responsible for outcomes after purchase.' It is, technically, all true. Why does it still stink, and what's the steady version?

It stinks because every sentence is a wall: each true fact is positioned to deflect rather than to answer. "Many customers have success" tells her she's the failure. "Healthy when sold" calls her account of the bush a lie without using the word. "Cannot be responsible" is a legal position taken against a $28 rose. She didn't write to litigate; she wrote because she's disappointed, and the reply treats disappointment as an attack.

The steady version:

"I'm sorry about the rose — it's a rotten feeling to plant something with hope and watch it fail. I can't say from here what happened; a few things can take a rose down in its first month, including a dry week right after planting. Bring in a photo of the bush and the spot where it's planted, and if it looks like the plant was weak, we'll replace it. If it looks like a planting issue, we'll show you what we'd do differently and still work something out on a replacement. Either way, come in — we'd rather have you gardening with us next spring."

Steady isn't soft: it still doesn't promise a refund, still asks for evidence (the photo), still distinguishes plant fault from planting fault. What changed is the stance — the reply now treats her as a gardener having a bad season instead of a claimant building a case. Defensive writing is usually factually fine and relationally catastrophic, because it answers the argument the writer feared instead of the message the customer sent.

Our farmers market's launch announcement paragraph feels flat: 'The market opens on May 3 at the fairgrounds. Vendors sell vegetables, baked goods, flowers, and preserves. Parking is available in the north lot. The market runs every Saturday until October.' Same problem as everyone's, I assume. Show me the rhythm fix.

Same problem, yes: four sentences of nearly identical length and identical shape — subject, verb, fact — a row of boxes. The rhythm fix, keeping every fact:

"The market opens May 3 at the fairgrounds. Vegetables, baked goods, flowers, preserves — forty vendors' worth, all of it from within fifty miles. Park in the north lot. Then come hungry, every Saturday until October."

What moved: the vendor list, which was a dutiful middle sentence, became a fragment with a dash and got the announcement's best fact added to its tail (forty vendors, fifty miles) so the long sentence earns its length. "Parking is available in the north lot" — nine words of officialese — shrank to a three-word instruction, "Park in the north lot," which does the same job at walking pace. And the season length, a flat fact in your closer, became part of an invitation ("come hungry") that lands the paragraph on the reader instead of the calendar.

Length pattern, before: even, even, even, even. After: medium, long, short, medium. That variance is most of what readers mean by "lively writing" — they feel it as energy, but it's really just sentences that don't all weigh the same.

I edit our HOA newsletter and the parking dispute has two camps. I need one paragraph reporting the board's decision that neither camp can accuse me of slanting. Facts: the board voted 4–1 to reserve six spaces near the clubhouse for guests; residents in Building C object that they lose their overflow parking; the board says the clubhouse lot is underused on weekdays; the rule starts June 1 with a review in September.

The paragraph:

"On Tuesday the board voted 4–1 to reserve six spaces near the clubhouse for guests, starting June 1. Building C residents objected that the spaces have served as their overflow parking, particularly on weekends. The board noted that the clubhouse lot is underused on weekdays and agreed to review the change in September, with the Building C concerns on the agenda."

The neutrality is mechanical, and that's why it will hold up: both positions are reported in the same grammatical form — a subject, a verb of saying, and their actual reason (weekend overflow; weekday underuse). Neither side gets an adjective. The losing side's objection is stated in its strongest specific form, not summarized as "some residents expressed concerns," which is how slant usually hides — one side gets reasons, the other gets *feelings*.

Two quiet choices to notice: the vote count (4–1) is reported because it's a fact both camps will cite anyway; reporting it yourself keeps it neutral. And the September review is given its agenda item — Building C's concerns, named — which tells the losing camp, in print, that they were heard and have a date. A neutral report can't give both sides the outcome. It can give both sides an accurate account of their own argument, which is what people mean, most of the time, when they say "fair."

It's our tenth anniversary and I want to write my wife a note, not a card. Everything I write sounds either like a wedding vow sequel or a thank-you note for services rendered. We've had a good, ordinary decade — two kids, a house that leaks, a lot of laughing in the kitchen. Help me find the register.

The register you're after is the anniversary note's own: it looks *back* with evidence and *forward* without promises it can't keep. Not vows (those are for beginnings) and not thanks (she's not a vendor). A draft in that register:

"Ten years. The house still leaks in the same corner, and I still say I'll fix it, and you still pretend to believe me — some of our best traditions are like that. What I actually know after a decade: the kitchen at 11 p.m., you laughing with a dish towel over your shoulder, is the center of my life, and everything else is arranged around it.
