I wouldn't trade the ordinary days. They're the ones I remember. Here's to the next ten — same kitchen, I'll get to the leak."

Why it avoids both failure modes: vows promise the future in grand terms; this makes one small joke-promise (the leak) that stands for all of them. A thank-you note lists services; this lists *scenes* — the towel, the laugh, the corner of the house — because a decade is stored as scenes, not services. And "I wouldn't trade the ordinary days" is the anniversary sentence vows can't say: it certifies, with ten years of evidence, that the unremarkable middle was the good part.

Restraint check: no "soulmate," no "best decision of my life" — she knows. The note's job at year ten isn't to convince her. It's to prove you've been paying attention.

In job interviews, my 'tell me about yourself' answer rambles: 'So I graduated in 2018, and then I worked at a call center, which was fine, and I did some training stuff there, and then I moved to Denver for a while, and I got into instructional design sort of by accident, and now I design courses, and I really like it, and I'm looking for something new, I guess.' Tighten it into something I can actually say.

Tightened to about thirty seconds spoken:

"I graduated in 2018 and started in a call center, where I ended up training new hires — that's where I found the work I actually wanted to do. I moved into instructional design from there, and for the past three years I've been designing courses for support teams. I'm looking for a role where training is the main job, not the side job."

The ramble's problem isn't length; it's that spoken answers get strung together with "and then... and then," which presents a career as weather — things that happened to you. The tight version replaces chronology with a *thread*: call center → training → design → this application, each step causing the next. Notice "sort of by accident" and "I guess" are gone — hedges that are honest in conversation but, in an interview, read as the candidate discounting their own story before the interviewer can.

What I protected: "that's where I found the work I actually wanted to do" — your one vivid, human sentence, the interview equivalent of a quotable core. Interviewers remember threads and one true sentence. Give them both, stop talking, and let them ask the next question — the ramble's last sin is that it never leaves room for one.

Last one. Our wedding program needs a short note about the ceremony. Brief we agreed: 'Audience: guests from both families, several meeting for the first time. Purpose: explain the handfasting part of the ceremony so nobody's confused when it happens. Register: warm, unhurried, zero stuffiness.' My draft: 'In accordance with an ancient tradition dating back centuries, the couple will partake in a handfasting ritual, wherein their hands shall be bound together with cord to symbolize their eternal union.' Run the final-voice check.

The check, brief line by brief line:

**Purpose — explain the handfasting so nobody's confused: PARTIAL.** A guest learns *that* hands will be bound with cord, but not the practical things confusion actually consists of: when it happens (during the vows), how long it takes (a minute), and that it's quiet — no participation required from the seats. Explanation means orienting, not just naming.

**Register — warm, unhurried, zero stuffiness: FAIL.** "In accordance with," "partake," "wherein," "shall be bound" — that's legal-ceremonial diction, the exact costume your brief banned. "Ancient tradition dating back centuries" says the same thing twice, and "eternal union" is a claim so large it stops meaning anything at a wedding, where smaller words carry more.

**Audience — both families, some meeting for the first time: FAIL quietly.** Nothing in the draft acknowledges a guest who has never seen this — no welcome, no "if you haven't seen one before," no reassurance that all they have to do is watch.

Passing version: "A note on one part of the ceremony: during the vows, Sam and June will have their hands loosely tied together with a cord — a handfasting. It's an old custom, it takes about a minute, and all you have to do is watch. The cord was braided by June's grandmother, which is the part they'd most like you to know."

Warm ("all you have to do is watch"), unhurried (short sentences, no rush of clauses), zero stuffiness — and the last line does the brief's deepest work: it gives two families, meeting for the first time, one shared, human fact to talk about at the reception. That's what program notes are for.
